Scene 1: Lichter-Wasser (Lights-Waters) 
1998-1999: No. 75 <Stockhausen-Verlag; cd SV-58) 
For soprano, tenor, and orchestra (solistic) with synthesizer; 2 transmitting micro­
phones, 29 microphone s, 4 x 2 loudspeakers, mixing console. 
Orchestra: 2 flutes, oboe, English horn, e flat clarinet, clarinet, bass clarinet, 2 bas­
soons, baritone saxophone, 2 horns; 2 trumpets, 2 trombon es, tenor horn, euphonium, 
tuba; 5 violins, 5 violas. 
Alternative title: "Sonntags-Gruss" (Sunday Greeting) 
Duration: 51'. 
This is no foyer greeting. It is Ylem with added voices, set in a rectangular 
space in which the seating has been arranged to resemble the British Union 
flag. Processing among the audience , tenor and soprano solo voices engage 
in an echo of medieval courtship dance in which the movements of king and 
queen, male and female, sun and moon, act out the mutually dependent 
orbits and obeisances of a celestial harmony. The music's polarities of high 
and low, and at times the harmonic language as well, hint at the symbolism 
of Kreuzspiel and Formel, but in this universe the tempered keyboards of 
glockenspiel, vibraphone , and celesta no longer occupy pivotal roles_ In their 
place are the two voices representing Michael and Eva, and it is they who 
move while the instrumen ts of the orchestra , in more cooperative mode than 
in "Orchester-Finalisten," stand quietly in their allocated positions among 
the audience , or looking on from galleries above, passing messages in klang­
farbenmelodie from one to another at the behest, so to speak, of the singing 
intelligences moving among them. 
Of his 1966 composition Terretektorh, in which the musicians of a large 
orchestra, each armed Momente-style with a simple percussion instrument, 
are distributed among the audience , Xenakis said 
... A radically new kinetic conception of music which no modern electro­
acoustical means could match .... The musical composition will thereby 
be entirely enriched throughout the hall both in spatial dimension and in 
movement. The speeds and accelerations of the movement of the sounds 
will be realized, and new and powerful functions will be [possible], such 
as logarithmic or Archimedean spirals, _ . _ [and] ordered or disordered 
masses, rolling one against the other like waves .... The listener will 
find himself . . . in a universe dotted about with little stars of sound, 
moving in compact nebulae or isolated. 2 
Stockha usen's instrumental forces are fewer in number, just twenty-nine to 
Xenakis's eighty-eight, and more subdued, but the imagery of planetary sys­
tems and waves of music following and interacting like waves of light is 
common to both: "12 MICHAEL -waves and 12 EVE-waves begin synchron­
ously, separate polyphonica lly, and meet at 7 further synchronous begin­
nings, connected by 6 bridges," as he puts it.3 
It is as though Stock hausen has taken the implicit spatial counterpoints 
and rotations of "Michaelion" (implying electronic projection to auditorium 
loudspeakers), and realized them in somewhat simplifie d form in real time 
and space. The three-dimensional distribution of instruments and voices is 
SONNTAG 487 
real and the audience is actually in the midst of the acoustic field. The mood 
is calm and relatively serene, the aesthetic a blend of curvaceous Jugendstil 
expressionism and the tactile purity of Bauhaus construct ivism. The two 
voices, singing texts more lucid and connected than usual, meet and inter­
twine in a form of palindromic counterpoint that is also medieval in origin 
and of a kind previously expressed in In Freundscha ft. As with the moving 
solo singers, so too Stockhausen's distribution of instruments reproduces in 
"real space" the virtual (electronically assisted) matrix of relationships only 
subliminally audible in "Michaels Reise," developments suggesting that the 
vocal and instrumental roles in "Lichter-Wa sser" are to be understood in the 
Kontakte sense as physical incarnations of previously immanent relation­
ships. 
The combination of male and female voices in this idyllic instrumental 
setting is both a distillation of the composer 's lifelong experience in spatial 
relations hips, and a return to a sense of spiritual purity, or to the primal 
innocence of a Garden of Eden in which the spatiality of Brant and the 
lyricism of Web ern are reconciled. What the title actually signifies is light of 
knowledge and water of life, but in the plural "lights" is also (tone-) colors: 
the fact that conventional orchestral instruments appear only in an accom­
panying, hence subordinate role in Sonntag, underscoring a message that 
"in the beginning was the word" (of command, of intelligen ce, of revelation), 
and that all other instruments are simply colors, or wordless derivations, of 
the singing voice. 
If so, it is a remarkable return to the Church's doctrinal position in the 
age of Gabrieli, which asserted that the only proper function of instruments 
was to double and support the voice, and that the sole purpose of the singing 
voice was to praise God. In the layout of "Lichter-Wa sser" one is inevitably 
reminded of the galleried musicians of the Elizabethan age, the heavenly 
choirs of Thomas Tallis, or of Heinrich Schutz-and indeed the polychoral 
motets for voices and instruments of the Venetian school-with the differ­
ence that Gabrieli, Montever di, and their contemporaries were taking 
exactly the opposite view from what Stockhausen now appears to be saying. 
Gabrieli's celebrated Sonata pian' e forte and other works like it were inten­
ded to usher in a new era of mobility of instrumental and tonal expression, 
freed from the restrictions of vocal range and of service to a sacred text.4 
Of all the scenes of LICHT, the music of "Lichter-Wass er" is among the 
most perfectly composed , in every sense. Restraint and refinement are keys 
to an unexpected depth of allusion, and iridescent color, gratefully assisted 
in the recordings by voices of a crystalline purity of tone and precision of 
delivery that the operas of LICHT have always asked for but not always 
received. 
From the opening introit for the two voices and synthesizer (the latter 
sounding more than ever like a small church organ), a listener is aware of 
undisguised tonality, literally a music of chromatic harmoni es. As the music 
unfolds, the old polarities of the Goeyvaerts era reemerge : one recognizes 
not only the mirror-imagery of high and low from Formel, but references to 
the relationship of voice and electronic music from Gesang der Jilnglinge , 
488 CHAPTER TWENTY-NINE 
now between voices and instruments , echoing the relationship of the two 
melody instruments of Kreuzspiel (oboe and bass clarinet) condensing in the 
middle register out of a cloud of points of piano and percussion converging 
from extremes of pitch. Banished is the fractured texture arising from serial 
dynamics, an entire parameter now restrained to a degree allowing the 
ensemble balance (and a listener's sense of space and directional play) to be 
more sensitively managed. 
In his handling of multiple-voice glissandi from the time of Montag aus 
LICHT, the composer has allowed brief and transitional accidents of tonal 
harmony to come to the surface. Now for the first time the tonal implica­
tions of the same polyphonic processes are positively emphasize d in a music 
of decorated cadences that seems finally to resolve the dramatic and 
philosophical contradictions of movemen t and cadence, of starting and stop­
ping (it is surely no coincidence that Stockha usen produced a revision of the 
1965 composition Stop, retitled Stop und Start, in 2001). Some of these 
cadential movements are plainly self-referential: at measure 318, and again 
at 530, chord "compressions" in the style of Dr. K.-Sextett; elsewhere, hints 
of the final chorale of Trans at 559, of Inori (not to mention a touch of 
Stravinsky's Symphony of Psalms) at 692, even a muted echo of Freitag's 
Bells of Monsalvat in the measures leading up to the closing cadence in g at 
728. The perceived effect of cadential movement gives the instrumental 
music here a welcome lightness and joviality, even under the admonitory 
direction of the two voices. The music is infused with a sense of discretion 
and tact, expressed especially clearly in the neo-Web ernian line of melody 
passing from one intrument to another, the same line heard to so lyrical a 
purpose in the London Sinfonietta recording of Kontra-Punkte, with whose 
amiable elegance of gesture the new work has much in common. 
The composer's good humor extends to a spontaneous repeat of the 
grand tutti at the Fourth bridge, measure 461, an Inori moment of palpable 
elation introduced by a soprano high d flat to the synthesizer timbre of a 
glockenspiel (or musical box), and ending in a well-deser ved (even if it is 
scripted) burst of applause. The repeat that ensues ("after such applause , 
wouldn't we want to repeat the Fourth bridge for one more time-and for 
the same money?" urges the soprano, clearly in exultant mood) leads her to 
climax on an even higher e flat, transcending into a new dimension to the 
accompaniment of a Messiaen-like coda of distinctly sugary harmonies , like 
outtakes from the Poemes pour Mi. 
Scene 2: Engel-Pr ozessionen (Angel Processions) 
2000: No. 76 <Stockhausen-Verlag; cd SV-67) 
For choir a cappella. 
Duration: 40'. 
At first glance, the idea of a conception as grand as LICHT concluding to a 
hymn of praise, in which groups of voices assume a succession of spatial 
configurations like movable letters in a toy acrostic on their way to spelling 
SONNTAG 489 
out an ultimate message of goodwill, seems a long way removed from the 
discarnat e visions of a Scriabin or a Kandinsky that the composer appears 
initially to have entertained. Though in every sense an ecstatic ritual, this 
does not seem at all like a music aspiring to the Artaudian delirium of a 
Boulez, the hallucinatory orchestrations of late Feldman or Scelsi, the reso­
nant emptiness of late Cage-not even the alien music conjured up by Louis 
and Bebe Barron to represent the vanished and disembodied superior 
intelligences of Altair 4 in the 1957 movie Forbidden Planet. Neverth eless, 
on the compose r's own ter ms, which after all have been shaped by a lifetime 
of involvement, through the atomization and reconstruction of language , 
with information science, the linguistics of Saussure, the structuralism of 
Piaget, and the legacy of linguistics in structural anthropology, the new 
work has to be regarded as a vocal tour de force of quite breathtaking 
genius. 
When composing for instrumental forces, Stockha usen preferred the 
broken consort to the instrumental family group of unified sonority. With a 
group of contrasting instruments there is a greater wealth of tonal possibi­
lities, and also the challenge of achieving harmony . Zeitmasse is not to be 
considered in terms of a uniform quintet of instruments of the same family; 
the "characteristic ensembles" of Stop are collections of deliberately (and to 
some ears, perversel y) variegated timbres; and even the string quartet of 
"Helikopter-Streichquart ett" is split asunder into unit soloists performing in 
separate enclosur es to the timekeeping of independent click tracks trans­
mitted from ground control. But while his inclinations instrumen tally tend 
toward diversity, in composing for voices Stockhausen has always seemed to 
recognize their potential for timbral as well as harmonic unity. Stimmung is 
perhaps the most notable example of a composition for an ensemble of voices 
treated in effect not just as the delivery system for a text of generalized 
praise, but as the ultimate living synthesizer. Over the years, this music in 
tum has attracted the attention of increasing numbers of specialized vocal 
ensembl es, many of them identifying equally with the intellectuall y deman­
ding polyphony of medieval, renaissa nce, and baroque eras, a European 
history in which (as we can now discern) music is understood as occupying a 
borderland between text and tone. Such ensembles identify with earlier 
conventions of harmonic and timbral unity associated with instrumental 
consorts of lutes, viols, recorders , and organ, and have evolved a tone of 
voice that is as well-adapted to Stockhausen as to Perotin, Machaut, Dufay, 
Willaert, and other composers of highly wrought polyphony . 
In their different ways, Webern's developmen t of a linear melody of tone 
colors, and Messiaen's explorat ion, most notably in his organ music, of the 
vertical dimension of colored resonances of unconventional mixture stops, 
can be reconciled as x and y coordinates of this third zone, between melody 
and harmony, in which timbre itself becomes an expressive variable for 
music, no longer just a random byproduct of speech. Since 1980, awareness 
of timbre as a variable dominated musical researches at IRCAM as well as 
the instrumental choices and orchestrations of Messiaen and Boulez. 
The sense of elation in "Engel-Prozess ionen" could be interpreted both 
490 CHAPTER TWENTY·NINE 
as a triumphant conclusion and as a sardonic and knowing criticism of the 
lack of progress in surround sound achieved by IRCAM's combined efforts of 
information science and computer technology in recent years. It recalls the 
triumphal subtext of Hymnen all over again: a demonstration of Stockhau­
sen's intellectual and musical pre-emine nce in the face of the best and most 
advanced developments science and technology have to offer. In 1966-67 the 
challenge was Max Mathews and the calculation of melodic probabilities; in 
2000 the equivalent challenges were voice modulation and the simulation of 
coherent movement in a three-dimension al space. In the new as in the 
earlier work, Stockhausen faces his opponents with a handcrafted musical 
artifact more advanced and more perfectly realized, both in a musical and in 
a technical sense, than anything his rivals were capable of achieving. For 
Hymnen the composer created an image of an artificial intelligence creating 
hybrid melodies out of national anthems; in "Engel-Prozession en" he con­
jures up an acoustic experience , in real time, of continuous linguistic and 
spatial modulation that the combined intellectual and computing power of 
IRCAM and MIT would dearly love to emulate, but could never hope to 
attain, at least for now. 
All of which is demonst rated, needless to say, under a cloak of the most 
brazenly unctuous and self-righteous religious sentiment that only a Stock­
hausen could get away with. Remember, too, that for all its richness of 
effect, the work remains a simulation of a process identified by the composer 
as one that has yet to be achieved , in the technical domain, even by himself. 
Transforming an admission of technical failure into an expression of master­
ful superiority involves the same logical inversion as Gesang der Junglinge, 
another work of genius that is also a disguised technical failure (in voice 
synthesis). Attaching a higher value by default to works aspiring to some 
sacred purpose, over the more modest but practical results of patient scien­
tific research, is oddly reminiscent of the policy aims, say, for German archi­
tecture under Albert Speer, which were to create sacred artifacts: tombs, or 
monume nts, or tombs in the style of monumen ts, in preference to structures 
for actual use.5 
Given the composer 's expressed impatience with twelve-tone "varia­
tions" or "suites" practiced by Schoenberg, Berg, and Webern-and even by 
Boulez, in Le marteau sans maUre-one is bound to note that "Engel-Prozes­
sionen" reverts once again to the sevenfold suite. The recording is disting­
uished by superbly disciplined singing, and the music-which for all of its 
complexity is singular ly grateful to listen to-by a number of genial inven­
tions. The excited temperament reaches back to the high spirits of Carre 
and Momente, but one wonders at the same time if the technical virtuosity 
of the vocal writing would have been conceivable without the composer's 
more recent trials of vocoder modulated soprano and bass voices. Although 
the choir groups are not mechanic ally modulated, Stockhausen's harmonic 
idiom has certainly developed stylistically in ways influenced by the vocoder 
and harmonizer employed in Freitag aus LICHT. These new techniques, 
including forms of heterophon y also familiar in ethnic music, are deployed 
with a wonderful looseness that accompanies bountiful self-confidence. 
SONNTAG 491 
Discretion and care in the placing and movement of musical sources 
within the horizontal plane are further welcome signs of a benign, and 
indeed, quietly radiant composure that no longer needs to make rhetorical 
demands on a performer's skills or an audience's patience . The animated 
and virtually continuous flow of text is literally colored by the distinctive 
textures of seven different languages into which Stockhausen's versicles of 
praise are translated . We are used to hearing Stockhausen in French, 
German, English, and (from time to time) the metalanguage of African­
American jazz, but the imaginative leap to include Persian, Hindi, Chinese, 
and Spanish is not only welcome from a diplomatic and musical point of 
view, but also as a paradigm shift to embrace real lan guages as an altern­
ative to the fractured syllables of earlier operas in the cycle that have 
proved such an obstacle to comprehension for singers and audiences alike. 
The settings of Chinese are truly wonderf ul: the inflection characteristics of 
the language proving especially congenial to Stockhausen's angular melody 
formations , and introducing a number of authentic and enchanting new and 
appropriate timbres, gliding inflections, and trills. A short verse in Swahili, 
associated with Samstag, is repeatedly delivered with a jovial and quite un­
Luciferian joie de vivre, at various times sounding more like the "Ur­
Sonate" of Kurt Schwitters than Schwitters himself. 
Of equal acoustic significance is the spatial opposition of moving choirs 
within the auditorium (along rectilinear aisles in conventional St. Michael's 
cross formation ), against a background of pianissimo "wall-sounds." This is 
an effect that would be understood and admired by the Venetian school. 
Stockhausen's lengthy period of reflection on conceptually necessary but 
dramatically challenging pedal points has resulted in an imaginative break­
through , the invention of a choral resonance that as well as producing 
harmonic effects of great beauty and subtlety, actually serves to enhance a 
listener's impression of spatial depth and presence. (It amounts in fact to a 
version for voices of Meyer-Eppler's "aleatoric modulat ion.") As recently as 
"Lichter-Was ser," the composer's use of sustained synthesizer harmonies to 
provide discreet coloration could not entirely allay suspicion that the instru­
ment's ulterior function was, well, to fill the gaps. Here, however, the "wall­
sounds," more than Fresco ever did, create a perfectly imagined and serene 
imagery of acoustic enclosure. 
Nothing is exaggerated. Everything works. The music ends with a 
"Schluss-Chor ale" of unbelievable richness. The overriding impression is, 
quite simply, glorious. 
Scene 3: Licht-Bilder (Light-Pictures) 
2002-3 : No. 77 (Stockhausen-Verlag; cd SV-68) 
For basset-hom, flute with ring-modulation, tenor, trumpet with ring-modulation, 
synthesizer, sound projectionist. 
Duration: 40'. 
The designer Johannes Conen, whose ingenious costumes for the metamor-
492 CHAPTER TWENTY-NINE 
phic couples brought a sense of Bosch-like fantasy and lightness of touch to 
Freitag aus LICHT, is collaborator in this work, premiered at the Donau­
eschingen Musiktage in October 2004. It is the final and only appearance in 
Sonntag aus LICHT of the instrumental trio representing the personae of 
Michael as trumpet er, Eva as basset-horn, and Ave as flute, here in delayed 
imitative relation with one another and a solo lyric tenor voice. The stage 
presentation combines video sculptures by Conen, moving in four temporal 
layers (revisiting the time-runners of Der Jahreslauf, but in the electronic 
domain), and spatial movement by the performers. Trumpet and flute are 
ring-modulat ed, but the basset-horn is not, perhaps because the charac­
teristic timbre of the reed instrument does not respond to ring-modulatio n. 
The composer describes the treatment as "double ring-modul ation," leading 
to a less noisy, but also less convincing result than Mantra or conventio nal 
ring-modulation employed in Mixtur. All the same, the composer's choices 
made it clear that the work is once again playing a looking-glass game of 
virtual (electronic) and real-time images of musical proc esses. 
In the event, the process of electronic refraction is associated with other 
kinds of splitting and fragmenting of musical materials: text into syllables, 
timbres into split waveforms, and melodies into fragments which are echoed 
one with another in canon. The effect is as though the participants are holo­
grams of players widely separated in space, originating in different time­
zones. One is reminded of the spatial separations of Helikopter-Streich­
quartett, and beyond to the time-delay effects of Solo from 1966, in which 
the concert performance is built up from a mysterious periodic convergence 
of voice layers at a single time and space, unrelated to the points of origin. 
The sense of communicating at light speed from distances of three to 
ten minutes (say, thirty to 100 million miles) is emphasi zed in practice by a 
style of part relationship that has little to do with civilized, or even formal 
dialogue, which involves a sense of give and take, listening to one another, 
and knowing when to stop. These voices tend to speak over one another, as 
though they cannot actually hear one another, and the broken texture of 
each-as if transmitted by bit-torrent by different routes-only adds to the 
confusion. Stockha usen had clearly studied Boulez's latest works in which 
instrumental lines are fragmented into onset, accent, and resonance compo­
nents to be shared among different timbres in appropriate combinations and 
times. In particular, Boulez's practice (acquired from Cage) of composing in 
syllables and fabricating new lines by interpolation and substitution, a 
technique applied to national anthems in Hymnen. Stockhausen's canons in 
the new work are as heavily disguised as Boulez, but grittier in texture and 
rather more challenging to interpret. 
On his admirable Stockha usen website Al Moritz compliments the com­
poser for his sureness of touch, while dismissing a live performance webcast 
of"Licht-Bilder" as technically inadequate . That may be true, but something 
is wrong when a stage performance technically directed by the composer 
sounds less than adequate for a listener outside the sweet spot. We have 
been here before, with "Michael ion." If Boulez can make it work, with the 
instrumen tal Memoriale (1986), it ought to be possible for a Stockha usen to 
SONNT AG 493 
organize a sound system for "Licht-Bilder" allowing the players to move 
freely, and distinguish direct from ambient sounds. An added difficulty, as 
with "Michaelion," arises with the choreogra phed rotation and movements 
of players. On the generous scale of "Engel-Prozes sion," slow-moving voices 
passing in front of fixed instruments in a suitable ample acoustic, is already 
traditional practice, making poetic sense, and easy, if subtle, to grasp. For a 
group of four players interweaving in tightly knit formations , on the other 
hand, lack of separation in real time and space creates avoidable congestion. 
The acoustic effect of orbiting players eclipsing one another, for example , 
may be enhanced by sound-absorbing baffies or columns onstage, behind 
which the players and their music are able to disappear from time to time. 
Scene 4: DOfte-Zeichen (Scents-Sig ns) 
2002: No. 78 (Stockhausen-Verlag; cd SV-69) 
For high soprano, soprano, contralto, high tenor, tenor, baritone, bass; boy's voice 
(treble), synthesizer; 8 transmitting microphon es, cd player, 7 loudspeakers, 4 monitor 
loudspeakers, mixing console. 
Duration: 58'. 
What comes vividly to mind is a memory of sharp smells, stale air, singing 
heads all around, and the curious timelessness of a caffeine-induced waking 
dream that comes over a listener at four in the morning after an early 
evening of recording has seamlessly passed into a night shift of adjusting 
levels. On the surface "Diifte-Zeichen" is just another public ceremony in the 
cycle of ceremonies of Sonntag aus LICHT, this time a rite of incense­
burning and naming that might easily be read as a trip back to the never­
never land of campfires and joss sticks. "The seven soloists sing about the 7 
scents and 7 signs of the days of the week. They burn the scents and explain 
the scents and signs," the composer explains .6 Below the surface, however, 
the combination of perfumes and disembodied voices evokes an anti-world of 
studio life in which the central character sits isolated behind a desk in a 
control room in the dead of night, playing back the same multiple tracks 
over and over, adjusting their relative positions-here a little to the left, 
there a little to the right-and the levels, up and down, searching for the 
ultimate balance. During this time the secondary voices continue to be 
heard in the background, rehearsing their lines as it were, waiting their 
time, signaling their presence and ready for attention. Through the control 
room glass you could see the vocalists , eyes firmly closed, a single head­
phone pressed against one ear, striving for the perfect inflection. Only by 
now the studio is empty, its lighting dimmed; the musicians long since 
departed, climbing out of a cab on the other side of town, tired and dingy, 
heading for bed. All that is left beyond the glass is a detritus of unattended 
microphones and discarded headphone s, empty water bottles, unfinished 
cartons of egg fu yong, and half-eaten hamburgers in paper napkins stained 
with ketchup and fat. Through speakers surrounding the mixing desk, the 
singers' disembodied voices continue effortlessly to sound, over and over, 
494 CHAPTER TWENT Y-NINE 
interrupted only by the lighting of another cigarette and the screech of re­
winding tape. 
The poetic of radio drama is as old as radio, and this is a portrait in 
music of an idealized radio drama, birthplace of electronic music, and a 
largely alien world to many listeners. Tyrone Guthrie, writing in 1929: 
There is no narration; scene and interlude follow one another without a 
break. After the end of each episode there should be a stroke of the bell, 
then the scream of a syren [sic], suggesting a rush through time and 
space. The "scenes" should be played very intimately in a rather low key; 
in contrast to the "interlud es," which are to be bold and reverberating .7 
Lance Sieveking, a contemporar y of Guthrie and pioneer BBC radio drama­
tist and producer, described the new art of voices as a music to be orches­
trated. Of his dialogue Intimate Snapshots, also from 1929, we read that he 
"so to speak, slow-motioned small pieces of speech in several places, 
sometimes in order to emphasise the meaning of the words as words, and 
sometimes in order to give them special significance as sound forms."8 
He admits that this may sound high-falutin, but says that he had in 
mind that moment of mental contact when people suddenly understand 
each other not only emotionally but intellectually. Sieveking might have 
added that he was here trying to present a radio equivalent of the ex­
changes of gestures and looks which can be witnessed at such moments 
on the stage. But, like Guthrie, he was seeking by such orchestration of 
speech to extend the dramatic range of expression which had become 
stereotyped. It must have seemed to [Val] Gielgud that these portrayals 
of social archetypes attended by choric interludes and slow-motion 
speech were aiming at some purely abstract form.9 
"Diifte-Zeichen" evokes an aural world of scents and disembodied voices 
moving in and out of conversation like a celestial diplomatic cocktail party 
(and even extending to traditional "moi-moi" greetings of symbolic affec­
tion). In ancient times a dialogue of unseen spirits would be perceived as the 
voices of the gods; today the prevailing caricature is of a Frankenstein labo­
ratory reeking of chemicals, containing an array of severed heads or brains 
floating in jars of saline solution, barely alive, longing for extinction, their 
endlessly circulating thoughts still connected to the world of the living by 
electrodes and threadlik e wires. A way of saying, to readers of a Romantic 
disposition, that images of eternity have their dark side, and a composer of 
Stockhausen's acute sensibilities is aware of the shadow and determined to 
acknowl edge that a voice preserved is also a voice doomed to wander forever 
in a timeless limbo: "auch Engel sind ewig unterwegs ," as the choir sang in 
Donnerstag. It also goes some way to explaining the absence of content of 
the composer 's libretti. 
There are two principal actions. One is Luzifer's return, snarling and 
honking like a disdainful Lord Haw- haw. The other is the presentation of a 
new Michael, picked out of the audience like a plant in a celebrity chat 
SONNTAG 495 
show. Both are reminders that there is, after all, life after LICHT, and that 
the dramatic tensions of the opera cycle are ongoing consequences of human 
life on earth. Since it is crucial to Stockhausen's message to bring home the 
reality of Michael , the Eva-persona (now a contralto), and Luzifer as living 
reincarnations and not voices from the past, it would make sense I think to 
present the alternate voices in a more disembodied way, in masks, or as 
celestial teleconf erencing faces on separate monitors, perhaps (the lips 
moving not quite in synch, like satellite interviews on television). The seven 
signs of the days are already proudly on display; to superimpose the seven 
singers' faces on the seven banners would not be entirely out of character. 
The work is scored for synthesizer (once again sounding like a modest 
church organ with limited, but elegant glissando effects) and the seven-voice 
ensemble, consisting of beautifully matched high soprano, soprano, alto, 
high tenor, tenor, baritone, and bass, that previously played a leading role 
in "Engel-Prozession en." (It is not hard to understand why the composer has 
since recommended that a performance of Sonntag aus LICHT be spread 
over three days, whatever havoc this might create for future planners of a 
festival of the entire week.) Toward the end of "Engel-Prozessionen" one 
hears a number of hints of the musical idiom of "Diifte-Zeichen": they 
include tight voice trills-a wonderful discovery, by the way-a clustered 
imitation of buzzing bees, a return of the multivoice water sounds of 
"Invisible Choirs," and metallic voice harmonics delicately drawn from a 
slow articulation of the diphthon gs of [Tiusd�], [Frmtag] , [MQntag], etc. The 
musical language of"Diifte-Zeichen" brings together elements of "Orchester­
Finalisten" (for example, animal impressions) with the new free-floating 
heterophon y and polyphony that have emerged out of the composer's long 
engagement with "rounds" (since "Atmen gibt das Leben ... "), and trials 
since then with the vocoder and harmonizer. The composer's handling of 
tempi and vocal textures, and his notation of them, is deceptively simple, 
but the gestural and harmonic vocabulary of Sonntag aus LICHT, here and 
elsewhere, is wonderfully subtle and refined. 
The music is sectioned into groups corresponding to the seven banners 
and scents, followed by a coda and "Annunciation" (probably the appropriate 
term) of a new Michael-in carnation. The seven cardinal divisions are further 
divided into segments treating the scent, the sign , and the essential char­
acter of the day in various voice combinations related to the spiritual status 
of the persona involved . In the setting of the composer 's texts (mostly in 
German and English), the prevailing style resembles a baroque cantata, 
alternating recitativ es, strictly harmonized chorales , and choruses of freer 
counterpoi nt. The supporting role of the synthesizer in all of this is remi­
niscent on the one hand of the chiming punctuations of Refrain, and on the 
other hand, of a Bach organ or harpsichor d accompaniment. Even after so 
many years, Stockhausen's ear for new harmonies has not deserted him; a 
new feature (also relating to Refrain, and perhaps also Adieu) is the frag­
mented undulation and dispersal by voices of the notes of a synthesizer 
chord, in the manner of ripples on a pond. 
Luzifer's reemergence into the light-very much alive and a force to be 
496 CHAPTER TWENTY-NINE 
reckoned with-is a little like Frankenstein returning to the laboratory for a 
recharge. In a music that inverts the earlier and almost tragic "Luzifers 
Traum" evocation of a spirit fading away, he bounces back in full snoring 
voice to deliver a stuttering "Samstag-Solo" in which, among other exple­
tives, the syllable "Rot" (red) mutates via a succession of hiccups (Rut, Blut, 
shoot, toot, etc.) to ud, Saturday's scent of the Indian eaglewood tree, finally 
to land (yes, you guessed it), on the formerly magic syllable "Hu!" 
Viewed in full array, Stockhausen's banner signs of the week, combin­
ing elements of the heraldic and the erotic, begin to resemble a Stravinskian 
deck of cards. What each actually signifies, as if that were not already 
obvious, is willy-nilly laid out in song, in verses of a blushing and overripe 
symbolism from the era of Aubrey Beardsley. They amount to a declaration 
that the range of gender preferences and combinations represented among 
the characters of LICHT is now fully compliant with the totality of modern­
day relationship practices-though it is hard to see Michael and Luzifer in 
any other than a stand-off relationship. 
In productions from the late nineties the name of Kathinka Pasveer 
appeared not only as a performing artist, but as an assistant in the record­
ing process itself. There is nothing unusual about that: somebody had to 
take on the task of carrying the compose r's aesthetic forward, and a second 
pair of ears is always a help. All the same, the recording of "Diifte-Zeichen" 
shows a few inconsistenc ies. While the bulk of the recording is very dry, the 
chorale- like tutti that follows immediat ely after "Sonntags-Duett" is sud­
denly reverberating like an empty gymnasium -an earlier take, perhaps . 
Added to which, an obvious and nasty edit affecting harmony and reverb­
eration at the entry point of the synthesizer immediat ely following, leading 
into the alto recitative (another glimpse of Bach, this time the St. Matthew 
Passion ) that forms a bridge between nocturnal limbo and the real world of 
Michael, the chosen one sitting amongst the audience.

In 1967 Stockha usen made sketches for a work of around 25 minutes in 
SONNTAG 497 
duration entitled Projektion fur Orchester, for large orchestra divided into 
nine mixed groups of 8-10 players. From the few pages that were fully 
orchestr ated before the project was abandoned , one can discover echoes of 
the final 1966 revision of Punkte 1952/1962, as well as anticipations of the 
layered structure and parallel harmonies of Trans. It had been Stock­
hausen's idea to have the piece performed in front of a film projection of the 
same orchestra playing the same work, the latter also performing against a 
filmed back projection of the same orchestr a playing the same piece, making 
a polyphony of one layer of "present tense" and two layers of "past tense." 
The musical material was designed, after the manner of the temporal layers 
of Solo, to allow the filtering out of different layers of music at different 
times, and also for performances at different tempi. 
Stockhausen's fascination with mirror-relationships, and in particular 
the implications of a live performance interacting with a complementary 
music that is prerecorded, or at least issuing out of a loudspeaker, short­
wave radio, or ring-modulat ion circuit, is oddly reminisc ent of the character 
Zelig from the movie by Woody Allen, a blank-faced Everyman with an 
uncanny compulsion to insert himself into the context of historic newsreel 
footage. This same interplay of the living with recorded history is revived in 
"Hoch-Zeiten," with the difference that this time the real face and the face 
in the mirror get to change places, a twist in the tale that could also be read 
as a paradigm shift that puts eternity on an equal footing with a continuous 
present-at least to the extent of allowing an ongoing dialogue between the 
"NOW" and the forever. Perhaps Sunday for Stockhausen is the day in 
which, as Carl von Weizsacker predicted , time ceases to exist, and "intensit y 
of experien ce will replace extensity." As well as meaning "marriage," the 
title "high-times" suggests not only the timeless moment of ecstasy (or "per­
petual high," as they say), but also the coincidence of all such moments 
across time. That very sentiment of unity of experience is also in harmony 
with the scene's manifest subtext of sexual union (which on this occasion is 
celebrated in verse rather than gesture), and equally with the compose r's 
profession of spiritual kinship with artists and compos ers of former times 
whose ideas have come to be realized in his composit ions. 
There is a residual irony, nevertheless, in the notion of a marriage that 
obliges the two parties to live in separate locations and commu nicate by 
radio. Stockhausen had previously floated the idea of a music performed 
simultaneously on different continents and communic ating by satellite, but 
we know from live telecasts from the other side of the world, that for a world 
even as small as our own the speed of light is still not fast enough to ensure 
the synchronization of ensembles in widely separated locations . That might 
not have been an issue for a modern Gabrieli writing in a canonic idiom 
designed to cope with freely variable time-delays , but it is certainly an issue 
for Stockhausen, whose layered structur e of five different tempi demands a 
degree of synchronicity available only among ensembles within the same 
time zone. 
This marriage is strictly between man and woman, and West and East, 
so the composers notes tell us; it is also a union of the temporal and the 
498 CHAPTER TWENTY-NINE 
eternal, and between voices and instruments, who we are invited to consider 
as compleme ntary aspects of vocal commun ication, singing being uniquely 
able to convey a text. Given that the pitch content available for the scene is 
extremely limited, Stockha usen has devised alternative ways of enriching 
his basic material. For voices, a return to coherent texts, some recycled from 
"Engel-Prozessionen," others newly invented, but also verses extracted from 
the Persian poet Hafiz (from Odes I, III, VI, VII, and IX, in the translation 
by John Nott), from the Indian Bilauamangala Staua, from a Chinese love 
poem, and other sources. For the sake of thematic consiste ncy the composer 
has grafted the name Michael, or Micha, or Michael-trumpeter, onto these 
original verses, and while these additions tend to look incongru ous in print, 
even in the International Phonetic Alphabet, and do nothing for the poetry, 
they blend well enough into the polyglot texture of the music. 
From a beautifully imagined beginning, a musical sigh of pleasure that 
works wonderfully in both the instrumental version (with choral insertions) 
and the choral version that comes later (with instrumental insertions), the 
celebration quickly expands in complexit y until both sides begin to resemble 
a Boulezian brainstorm, or indeed a Cageian circus. The temptation to go 
with multiplic ity and density of effect rather than restraint is understand­
able, but given the potential for subtlety of movement in differing tempi, 
and bearing in mind the work's structural affinity with the five-part caden­
zas of Zeitmasse , for example, it seems at times like overkill. 
Though based on a very limited repertoire of precise tonal centers, the 
verse-set ting itself, on the other hand, is inventively realized in a form of 
decorated sprechstimme in which the central tone or accent (in Messiaen 's 
terminology) corresponds to the formula pitch, while the anacrouse and 
desinence are modeled after typical inflections of the chosen language. 
Stockhausen is clearly enamored of the sounds and rhythms of Chinese and 
Swahili, which he employs with enthusia sm. The graphic notation is not 
difficult in itself; what is a challenge is the timing of the temporal layers, 
controlled from spoken click-tracks via earpieces. In performance the super­
imposition of layers is often so dense, and the underlying pitch material so 
inert, as to give the illusion of a much simpler common tempo. The overall 
tempo-schema is essentially a tempered scale in which the frequency inter­
val between successive steps is in the ratio roughly of 4 : 3 (MM 30, 40, 53.4, 
71.2, 95.6, 134, 180). Not quite, I think, the classic tempo-scale from the era 
of Kontra-Punkte, as the composer's notes appear to claim, but rather an 
ascending scale in approximate fourths, as in Studie II, Kontakte, or Mant­
ra, or Schoenber g's Kammersymphonie. 
Five groups of singers, and their compleme ntary five groups of instru­
mentalist s are arranged in corresponding arc formations on their respective 
platforms. Groups I, of treble instruments and singers, are situated to the 
right, the others in order through to Groups V, bass instrumen ts and 
singers, to the left. Medieval convention would tend to associate the higher­
pitched with heaven on the left, and the lower-pitched with hell on the right, 
but what we have here is a return to a layout after the baroque keyboard of 
Kreuzspiel and Spiel. Suspended above the front of each platform, Trans 
SONNTAG 499 
fashion, are five louds peakers that relay the music from the corresponding 
unseen group in the other place-a classic arrangement from the world of 
Harvey Fletcher and Leopold Stokowsi in the 1930s. There is a manifest 
symmetry of instrumental and choral ensembles, and they perform from the 
same tonal material, embroiderin g it in different characteristic ways, so 
that when the sound of one group breaks through, as it were, into the other 
performance space, the music is essentially the same to a point where the 
listener should be able to hear transitions from inarticulat e inflections into 
articulate speech, or singing voices into instrumental tones-literally depen­
ding on where the audience and music are coming from. 
It is good to recall that this work marked a restoration of relations , 
hence a reconciliat ion, with Cologne Radio, and to hear Stockha usen com­
posing with evident goodwill and high spirits for a coherent body of conven­
tional instruments , organized in multiples of the same instrument. A layout 
of timbre-clusters facing one another suggests rich possibilities of dynamic 
intermodu lation, and the nature of the heterophonic material itself would 
offer scope for the kind of delicate transient effects previously encountered 
in Adieu, and at least hinted at in the two-voice Indianerlieder. Composed 
interference effects, vocal or instrumental, have disappeared, however, in 
the turbu lence of the moment. Of the musical action it might be observed, 
not for the first time, that it seems to pass directly from a magical onset to 
an extended fade without deliverin g much by way of a mission statement in 
between, but the elusiveness of the content is a large part of the music's 
implication and charm, and the high spirits are certainly palpable. 
The recording on compact disc is close-set and contradictorily lacking in 
the antiphonal distance suggested both by the physical separation of the two 
ensembl es, and by the dramatic conception of worlds at once conjoined and 
apart. It seems that, as in the recording of Trans, Stockhausen has opted, as 
in some others of his more recent recordings , to create as exact a super­
imposition of the two worlds as possible, despite their separation in reality. 
A by-product of arranging the two groups of performers by pitch across the 
stage is that the center of gravity, in terms of frequency, seems displaced 
toward the right side, a tendency not altogether helped by equalization of 
some of the lower-pitched instrume nts to darken the tone, making the cellos 
sound in places like double-ba sses. The entire instrumentat ion, to be sure, 
reverts to the triples of the Formel era, a decision perhaps making aesthetic 
sense for the end of a cycle that is both personal and global, but one that 
raises the old specter of an inherently unbalanced totality. 
Sonntags-Absch ied (Sunday Farewell) 
2001-2003 : No. 80 (Stockhausen-Verlag cd SV-74)

Strahlen (Rays)

Whereas "Licht-Bilder" resembles a teleconference of holograms converging 
on the same venue in artificial space, meeting but not consciousl y inter­
acting, the title "Strahlen" (rays or streams of light) suggests its opposite, a 
simultaneous projection of multiple sound signals from a common point of 
origin to the ends of the universe. As a musical idea, "Strahlen" sounds like 
space music from the era of Flash Gordon. It revisits the "sine-tone fa rewell" 
moment from Hymnen Region IV (beginning at 18' 04,2"), an authentic and 
in retrospect genuinely moving dialogue of sine tones in the spirit ofVarese, 
seeming to pierce the darkness like searchlights scanning the night sky. 
While "Strahlen" evokes the sound-world of Refrain, the timeless composur e 
of the earler work is abandoned , replaced (perhaps tongue in cheek, who 
knows?) by sounds suggesting the amiable chatter and whistle speech of a 
sci-fi movie robot. The powerful suggestion of limitless radiance in the new 
title is compromised in practice, not just in the players being required to 
imitate the phonemes and texture of speech, but the composer 's insistence 
on maintaining the exact rhythms and inflections of human speech in real 
time, creating a dense texture of simultaneous voices without suggestion of 
meaningful interaction or indeed, relativistic red-or blue-shif ting. That the 
texture of speech is treated as a constant and only the respective tempi of 
different languages as a variable, sits oddly with current astronomy, where 
messages are received in the light of distant star systems, and decoded from 
the displaced absorption lines of frequency-shifted spectra. 
While names of planned but unwritten works can suggest a flavor of 
intent, results in practice can change in response to difficulties arising in 
execution, which is again the case her e. Both realizations, "Strahlen" and 
"Sonntags-Abschied," while based on a reworking of the identical polyphony 
of languages of "Hoch-Zeit en," are very different species, the version for five 
synthesizers evoking a world of inner space and meditation rather than 
sending electronic messages out into the void. As gestures of farewell both 
works, while multidimensional in implicat ion, amount to monoph onic in 
experien ce. Neither manages to attain the widescreen, overwhelming scale, 
for example , of Louis and Bebe Barron's "electronic tonalities" for the movie 
Forbidden Planet (1956), even while employing essentially the same vocab­
ulary of gliding tones as the earlier work (in the former case, by electric 
guitar). A comparison tends to favor the more physical sound of an electric 
guitar, an instrument traditionally more responsive in the hands of a solo 
performer than an electronic keyboard whose gliding tones are controlled by 
a foot pedal, or turning a knob on the instrument's dashboard. 
The challenge set by the composer is of transforming the characteristic 
tone qualities and inflections of speech into synthesized tone gestures. Such 
a task reverts to the age of Gesang der Jiinglinge , with the key difference 
that the performers themselv es are now required to provide both means and 
answers, a delegation of responsibilit y on the part of the composer amoun-
SONNTAG 501 
ting in effect to a vote of no confidence , or very little, in the modern synthe­
sizer (with the exception perhaps of Simon Stockhausen's textured sounds 
for Freitag aus LICHT) . 
A report by Richard Toop, observing preparatory rehearsals for the first 
performance in August 2004 of the version for five synthesizers, describes 
the composer's interactions with the performers of a younger generation, all 
born around 1970, in terms of mounting impatience , perhaps even despair, 
at the unawareness among the young of the past history of sound and voice 
synthesis represented by Stockhausen's own works, and their indifference to 
the tactile expressive dimension of analogue synthesis compared to digital 
sampling and processing. To imitate speech sounds, one has to understand 
speech processes, in short by studying them. Even the theremin from 1928 
was capable of voicelike inflection, being subject, like the violin, to manual 
control. Stockhausen's criticisms of the present generation of synthesizer 
players are directed ultimately at the suppression of analogue technology, 
and domination of synthesizer practice, at IRCAM and elsewhere, by a US 
philosoph y of digital synthesis adopted and marketed by Japan, based on 
samples and presets: "a thing of threads and patches," as the minstrel sings 
in Gilbert and Sullivan's Mikado. 
At the time of its initial conception, the choice of "Strahl en" as a title 
might have hinted at the possibility of global destruction by radiation (out of 
which LICHT was intended to survive as an encrypted legacy of twentieth­
century Western culture). The danger of such an eventuality having reced­
ed, in spite of Chernobyl and subsequent events (among which the Berliner 
Festspiele's scheduling of the official German premiere on the third anni­
versary of 9/11 might have been misinterpreted), the tone of the work, in 
keeping with earlier scenes, is benign rather than confrontational . At the 
very least, the most up-to-date version of Josef Matthias Hauer's "modern 
orchestra" provides a rich resource in principle for timbral counterpoint and 
manually controlled lateral (and even vertical) movements of sound in 
space, if rather less opportunity for their spatial deployment in a concert 
setting. Stockhausen's collaboration with Antonio Perez Abelian succeeded 
in refining the range of tone colors and textures available to the synthesizer, 
though leaving the instrument still unable to match the physical presence of 
electronic sounds from the early tape era, a conseque nce of design principles 
focused on waveform simulation to the exclusion of all other concern with 
the physical nature of traditional instruments as signal generators and 
cavity resonators. It would not be too much perhaps to hope that a future 
edition of the work might succeed in creating virtual sonic images moving in 
a three-dimensional space through the mutual interference of otherwise 
inaudibl e frequencies. Or more realistically, given the indications of Piano 
Pieces XVI and XVI I, a version in the original spirit of Carre and Kontakte, 
perhaps even Kurzwellen, in which a principal solo keyboard interacts with 
four ancillary synthesizers to create a dynamic polyphony in which gestural 
and timbral imitation, supplemented by a degree of inspired intuition, are 
the defining features. 
An array of five synthesizers of the same manufacture and model to 
502 CHAPTER TWENT Y·NINE 
provide a send-off to participants of the crowning event of the entire LICHT 
cycle is bound in any case to provoke comparison with the six solo acoustic 
keyboard instruments who provide an analogous upbeat finale to Boulez's 
Repons of 1984. In the Paris showpiece melody sequences (effectively arpeg­
giated note sequences running in ascending scales) are intercepted in real 
time by a central computer and interpreted as instructions to trigger oscil­
lating responses in the form of permutations of the same or different note 
sequences . It is all very impressive, except that the solo players' ascending 
melodies are all selected from the equal-temper ed scale, and correspond in 
Midi terms to number sets represen ting keys. This ingenious technology 
deriving from Max Mathews' GROOVE synthesis and implemen ted by US 
and Japanese synthesizer manufacturers is the same technology and associ­
ated vocabulary of matte metallic tones chosen by Stockhausen for his five­
piece synthesizer chorus to end Sonntag aus LICHT. It is a daunting task to 
have delegated to a younger generation, and a challenge, looking forward, to 
adequately fulfill. We encounter similar interactions of oscillating melodies 
in conversational exchang es, in the KLANG cycle of trios, culminating in the 
brain explosion of Cosmic Pulses. 
CHAPTER THI RTY 
Last Rites 
After completing the week-long celebration of LICHT Stockhausen deter­
mined to devote the new KLANG cycle, honoring the hours of the day, to 
chamber works appealing to a wide range of instruments , a pragmatic 
decision in part to bolster the Stockhausen Verlag catalog ue. After consider ­
ing "Liebe" (Love) and "Night and Day" as overall titles, the composer 
decided on "Klang," which has prior ass ociations with Momente and charac­
ters K, M. D (Klang, Melodie, Dauer), alluding to Karlheinz , Mary, and 
Doris. The word "hours," as in "Les tres riches heures du Due de Curtine," 
refers to times of day allotted to prayer and meditation, not to actual 
durations. The pieces are all the same meditations in the medieval sense: 
brief catechisms on the subject of time, ruminated at length. 
For the composer, whose health had been deteriorating for a number of 
years, the likelihood of surviving to complete another cycle of large-scale 
works, however appealing in principle , was fast diminishing. His mental 
energy and resilience appeared as strong as ever, but physically he was 
worn out, and his heart was failing. Knowing nothing of his condition, I was 
taken aback in 1989 to see how much the composer had physically aged in a 
small portfolio of Clive Barda photographs supplied for selecting a cover 
illustration for Stockhausen on Music. Months later, a sepia-tinted snap­
shot chosen by the designer for the cover of the 1990 edition of The Works of 
Stockhaus en, drawn from press coverage of the Harrogate Festival , pictured 
an uncharacteristically downcast composer perched at the edge of an empty 
stage, gazing at the floor-a far cry from the tense face, piercing gaze, and 
triumphant Cheshire cat grin of former times. 
A sense of borrowed time hovers over much of LICHT, starting with the 
stylistically not to mention thematically improbable recycling of Der Jahres­
lauf in Dienstag aus LICHT, by way of the unending sevenfold suites of 
Freitag, to the unabashed duplication of whole scenes by voices and instru­
ments, or live and electronic identities, in Mittwoch and Sonntag. Images of 
split brains, or identities, in which the same music appears in different 
guises representing mind and body and it is the performers' task to bind 
them together, become a persistent theme. At the Birmingham premiere of 
504 CHAPTER THIRTY 
Mittwoch in 2012, the art deco formality and solemnity of Litanei 97-a 
choral setting of a recycled 1968 text from Aus den sieben Tagen-felt and 
sounded like a last testament (which of course it always was). A growing 
sense of the pressures of mortalit y may have prompted the composer at 
times under interview to seek refuge in the prejudices of an earlier life, 
leading to lapses of diplomac y in public relations. His unguarded comment s 
on the 9/11 attacks can be understood to express admiration for the artistic 
integrity of those who choose to die on their own terms in pursuit of an ideal, 
however perverse-a sentiment associated with both Walter Benjamin and 
Theodor Adorno.l A sense of imminent departure from the world of the liv­
ing adds a layer of emotion to certain scenes-and in the case of Mittwoch , 
to an entire opera, each scene of which deals in a different way with a theme 
of absen ce, or departure, suspense, or loss and replacement of a leader. 
To follow Sirius, the year, and LICHT, the week, the prospect of a cycle 
of works based on the hours of the day had been aired as long ago as 1982, 
in conversation with Rudolf Frisius.2 At that time the idea was consistent 
with the composer's express concern with "going ever further into the micro­
structure of a wave," an objective since the time of the Konkrete EtUde in 
1952. After the hour, the minute, and after the minute, the second, projects 
suggesting alternative scales of perception, in fast or slow motion, compared 
to the pace of normal life. By 2003, however, a work schedule of twenty-f our 
new pieces, each representing an hour, called for drastic simplifications and 
economies in planning, addressed with even greater urgency in 2007. Under 
the draft title LIEBE (Love) a preliminary sketch assigns twenty-four colors 
to the pieces, the pencilled footnote "24 Stundenkla nge auch gleichzeitig " 
(24 Hour-sounds also simu ltaneous) suggesting a cycle of works open to be 
presented on the same day at multiple locations, in parts perhaps even at 
the same time.3 Such a view is reinforced by the later decision to make the 
layered structure of Cosmic Pulses a foundation of the "Urantia Hours," and 
is consistent in a slightly different sense with the decision to explore recom­
binations of the trio SchOnheit in six alternate trio formations. 
The title Klang eventually chosen, an outwardly undistinguished word 
in German (meaning: sound or timbre), makes particular sense in English 
as a term "clang" selected in 1875 by Sedley Taylor, a disciple and contem­
porary of Helmholtz, to describe a complex tone such as a bell, the partial 
tones of which are inharmon ic.4 It is one of the stranger realities of 
acoustics that a bell is fashioned to be out of tune with itself in order for its 
vibrations to continue to resound for as long as possible. A bell whose par­
tials are in harmony is liable to fracture, and its tone to die away rapidly. 
The implications are many and various, but revolve around the notion that 
difference leads to interaction, and interaction on multiple levels to prolong­
ing the life of the tone. A "simultaneous concert" of multiple works playing 
in different time zones around the world has its own special appeal, after 
the mirror-image play of "Hoch- Zeiten" performing in different locations , 
and delayed canons of "Lichter-Wasser" suggesting distance in space as well 
as time. The idea awakens memories of earlier trials of multiloc ation 
compositions at the time of Ensemble and Musik fur ein Haus. In principle, 
LAST RITES 505 
for KLANG to work as a multilayered unity, the various Hours should be 
musically compatible, if not exactly in harmony. And sure enough, compa­
tibility is implied, if not guarantee d, by a common twelve-tone series of two 
hexachords , reciprocal note collections corresponding to alternat e pitches of 
an all-interval series recommended by Herbert Eimert in his Lehrbuch der 
Zwolftontechnik (1950). 
LICHT is a composition of seven days of tone and color relations in 
association with the seven-color spectrum of Goethe. To match the 24 hours 
of KLANG with an equivalent light spectrum Stockhausen chose a twen­
tieth-century cycle of 24 colors devised by Wilhelm Ostwald, a scientist and 
supporter of the Munich art group Die Brucke, whose theory of color rela­
tions influenced the modern art of Paul Klee and Piet Mondrian. It is not 
entirely clear how Ostwald's color circle, which is about visual perception, is 
reconciled with Goethe's prior definition of the spectrum as contaminations 
of light with darkness, which incorporates a moral hierarchy. The entire 
idea of a closed circle of light frequencies is a charming fiction in any case, 
since the frequencies of light, like sound, form a linear scale from infrared to 
ultra-violet, lower to upper limits of human perception, a ratio of light freq­
uencies closer incidentally to a minor sixth than an octave in ratio. 
A composer 's last works are often read as settling old scores. KLANG is 
open to interpretation in the same spirit as Stravinsky's Agon: a suite (yes, 
a suite) of characteristic pieces wrapped around a sequence of dance forms 
presented as serial permutations of male and female dancers, under a title 
signifying a struggle or contest, the task in Stravinsky's case to master the 
twelve-tone system at an advanced age. As "last works," KLANG has attrac­
ted more than its share of mystical commentary, alleging on the one hand a 
return to the Catholic faith of his youth, and elsewhere of the compose r's 
ultimate adoption and commitment to the articles of the Urantia Founda­
tion. Neither advocacy group appears to recall Stockhausen's earlier protes­
tations of originatin g from the Sirius star system, a mere speck in the 
Urantia cosmos. An observer may choose to dismiss the composer 's (or his 
acolytes') solemn pieties as distractions or masks, intended to cover their 
own nakedness, or shield the music from inquiry. One does not have to 
doubt the composer 's good faith to recognize that the emulation of religious 
ritual is an effective means of persuading a lay audience to sit still and show 
respect. 
Among some commentat ors, however, a fixation on religious symbolism 
has been used to isolate conversation of the KLANG cycle from the record 
and context of the composer 's artistic history, along with lifelong technical 
interests and loyalties. In the past, Stockhausen has freely amplified his 
liner notes with information on the technical setup for a given recording, 
identifying microphones and speakers, and crediting engineers by name, all 
of which is useful and admirab le, while at times reproducing detailed circuit 
diagrams and mixing desk settings, not all of which are equally helpful. The 
marked avoidance of technical detail in relation to works of the KLANG 
cycle can be understood sympathetically as a consequence of the speed with 
which they were composed and recorded; all the same, the absence identifies 
506 CHAPTER THI RTY 
the last works as "works in progress" or prototypes in the sense of not 
having fully unde rgone the routine stages of practical and technical feed­
back, and design adjustments and modific ations to the score, that one would 
normally expect. 
The cloak of religiosity spun around these last works has allowed a new 
generation of opinion formers to publish tendentiously and at length about 
imaginary spiritual clues and messages in the last works, at the same time 
ignoring their connection and contribution to the totality of Stockhausen's 
output, and beyond it to contempo rary music in general. An example: the 
composition Freude for two harpists is presented to the world as a work of 
sublime kitsch featuring two lady harpists singing like angels at their 
instruments , the latter juxtaposed in the shape of a Valentine's Day heart. 
Behind the cute fac;ade, however, is a toughly written and frankly playful 
reprise of the sounds and textures of Piano Piece X, leaving an impression of 
the new work having been created as a parting gift to Boulez, the supremely 
rational composer in 1998 of Sur Incises, a frantically scurrying decons­
truction of piano tone for three pianos, percussion, and three harps . There is 
little if any religiosity to be drawn from the dry, matter-of -fact litanies of 
names and locations incorporated in the electronic layers like Post-it notes, 
or fridge magnet poems assembled from scraps of memories like monologues 
from Samuel Beckett. (A real if only justification for Stockhausen's adoption 
of Urantia names and titles is that they provide a framework for mysticism 
without running the risk of giving offense to any actual religion.) 
In the final years of completing LICHT, Stockhausen acquired WDR 
tapes of Momente (a 1998 performance directed by Rupert Huber), and a 
2004 performance of Punkte conducted by Peter Eotvos, for issue under the 
Stockhausen Verlag label. In 2001 he recomposed Stop, a Feldmanesque 
study dating from 1965, the era of Mixtur (itself a Morton Feldman inspired 
composition with added ring modulatio n). The new work was Stop and 
Start. "A model for moment form" wrote the composer in the briefliner notes 
for the 2002 cd. All of which indicates that while putting the final touches to 
Sonntag aus LICHT, Stockhausen was consider ing a return to moment 
form, a music of vertical instants rather than linear exposition and devel­
opment. This is where Feldman comes into the picture. Stockha usen's slices 
of time express a process analagous to the movies, expressed in acoustical 
terms. In traditional narrative the listener is led through a temporal 
experience by a narrative unfolding in lockstep with the events described . In 
moment-form a distinction is created between the reader's experience, a 
temporal process, and the object of contemplation or artwork, which rem­
ains unchanged but is mysteriously transformed by the act of attention. In 
short, Stockhausen was revisiting and renewing past ideas of "point" form 
and "moment" form, implying a renewed intention to employ a new gene­
ration of synthesizers as a means of further exploring, analyzing, or in other 
ways prolonging the instant of illumination.
