Himmel fahrt (Ascension) 
2004-5: First Hour of KLANG. No. 81 (Stockhausen-Verlag; cd SV-83) 
For organ or synthesizer, soprano, and tenor. 
Duration: 37'. 507 
The title arises out of terms of commission for a work to be premiered on 
Ascension Day. For Stockhausen, as for the Schoenberg of Die Jakobsleiter, 
ascension is associated with spiritual self-impr ovement, which is a tough 
call, rather than being carried passively aloft by divine escalator. To earn a 
place in heaven the keyboard player is obliged to master a score in which 
left and right hands are assigned different tempi. Male and female singers 
are present on either hand to assist in the task of harmonious discon­
nection by reciting an overripe litany of words of encouragement reminis­
cent of former teacher Olivier Messiaen in devotional mood. We have been 
here before, for example , in Poemes pour Mi: 
Le Ciel, 
Et l'eau qui suit les variations des nuages, 
Et La terre, et les montagnes qui attendent toujours, 
Et La lumiere qui transforme. 
The idea of a music of multiple layers coexisting at different tempi is hardly 
new. Elliott Carter devoted the last years of an immensely great age to 
inventing witty duos combining more or less unrelated tempi. Stravinsky's 
Owl and the Pussy-cat does the same for solo singer and piano accompanist. 
To insist that the left and right hands of the same solo keyboard player keep 
independent time might appear to be twisting the knife. Conlon Nancarrow 
succeeded by punching his own piano rolls. Stockhausen had previously att­
empted the same in Intervall, a text composition from Fur kommende Zeiten 
for one piano and a duo of blindfolded pianists. The keyboardist's task in the 
present case is made more than usually academic in several ways: 1. the 
printed score visually aligns the two hands exactly on the same page, allow­
ing the player to "juggle and adjust" as Stravinsk y said of the conductors in 
Gruppen; or 2. the player can rewrite the score, as players and conductors 
do, even with the compose r's blessing, as recently as the first performance of 
Sonntags-Abschied. More to the point, 3. the organ or synthesizer, unlike 
the piano, inherently lacks touch, so the mental task of carrying two tempi 
at once, while creating unnecess ary stress for the player , is to all intents 
and purposes acoustic ally meaning less. In the official cd edition for synthe­
sizer, the visual simplicity of the two-handed score is sonically camouflaged 
by a choice of mixture stops in undistinguished parallel harmonies (the 
same or similar mixtures reappearing in Cosmic Pulses). A critical absence 
peculiar to the organ is a scale of accents and variations in touch, of the 
kind employed in Messiaen's Mode de valeurs or Stockhausen's piano pieces 
from the 1950s. Accents signify little in the context of organ or synthesizer 
tone , and what programmed touch distinctions are available, are erased as 
the composer insisted during rehearsals for the premiere of Sonntags-
508 CHAPTER THIRTY 
Abschied . Finally, 4. the composer himself long ago instructed performers of 
his Piano Pieces I-IV to play "as fast as possible" and convert his famously 
complicated notated rhythms into tempo changes , implying no difference 
between the two, a precedent for rewriting the tempo changes of the present 
work back into divisions of a common tempo. 
The sense of mental detachment associated with the idea of indepen­
dent hands is all the same real, a natural consequence of comparing live 
performer actions with a recording. It might be an interesting challenge, for 
instance, to have the work performed by a right -handed player on a repro­
ducing piano set up (perhaps even by another pianist) to reproduce the left 
hand invisibly . To experience a concert performance of Piano Pieces I-IV (or 
even Piano Piece X) executed by reproducing piano without the distracting 
presence of a live performer offers fresh and vivid insights into the works' 
structure, as one may attest from piano rolls of the past (a performance of 
Stravinsky's Rag-Time by a Bosendorfer grand on YouTube coming readily 
to mind). The printed score of Boulez's "Constellation-Mir oir" from his Third 
Piano Sonata, a dialogue of "points" and "blocks" in red and green, might 
gain from being interpreted stereo fashion by two performers on separate 
pianos, one playing red, the other green. The prospect of hearing Piano Piece 
XI performed on multiple reproducing pianos scarcely bears thi nking about. 
Freude (Joy) 
2005: Second Hour of KLANG. No. 82 (Stockhausen-Verlag; cd SV-84) 
For 2 harps (who also sing). 
Duration: 41'. 
A delightfully athletic showpiece for matching harps, with unrealized poten­
tial for stereophonic interpretati on, the two instruments virtually over­
lapping on the platform, suggesting left and right stereo images in invisible 
unity. One is reminded in places of the "fast rewind" coda of Mantra for two 
pianos, and overall of the musical rhetoric of Piano Piece X, its lion's roar 
tamed and feminized. The tone quality is rounded and uniform, a nylon 
rather than gut tone quality giving the ensemble a blended evenness and 
tactile presence reminiscent of a Bach era Lautenwerk. The outward solem­
nity of the occasion is touchingly redeemed by a genuine emanation of high 
spirits. 
NatOrliche Dauern 1-24 (Natural Durations 1-24) 
2005-6: Third Hour of KLANG. No. 83 (Stockhausen-Verlag; cd SV-85A-B) 
For piano. 
Duration: 2 hours 21'. 
Alfred North Whitehead identified point, moment, and rect as dimensions of 
time. A musical meditation on the experience of time passing revisits the 
era of Stockhausen's essay " ... how time passes ... ". A point has position 
but no magnitude; a moment has extension but no development (which 
LAST RITES 509 
would imply duration), while the term reet signifies extension in time by 
virtue of continuous change, for example a sound dying away. Punkt and 
Moment are familiar concepts in Stockhausen's music: one recalls that he 
studied philosophy at university. The term reet is less obviously linked to 
the composer, other than by association with the text composition Richtige 
Dauern from the collection Aus den sieben Tagen. In turn, the drawn-out 
tones of NatUrliehe Dauern recall Refrain, the 1959 composition for a trio of 
keyboards in which the timing of events alternates between extremes of as 
long as it takes for a sound to die away naturally to a specified minimum , 
and as fast as possible, the longer tones testing the acoustic of the ensemble 
in the manner of a specialist timing the reverberation of a concert hall. 
For the cd recording pieces 1-15 are performed alternately by Frank 
Gutschmidt and Benjamin Kobler, in an impression of anglers casting into 
the stillness of a lake from opposite ends of the same dinghy, after waiting 
for previous ripples to die away. The sense of space is a welcome relief, like 
the tocsins of Turin but relying on instrumental rather than manufactured 
effects. Inevitably the combination of measured attacks and attractively 
animated resonances, mostly arising from the inharmonicities of tempered 
tuning, acknowledges Feldman, composer of Madame Press died last week at 
ninety, a work in honor of his piano teacher in the acoustic image of an 
elderly cuckoo-clock plaintively chiming the same hour of duty day in, day 
out. An impression lingers that sharing duties between two players intro­
duces a subtle element of visual drama. The remaining pieces 16-24 are 
dedicated to, and performed by Antonio Perez AbelIan. Despite having been 
recorded in the same WDR studio, and presumably on the same instrument, 
the balance on the second cd is subtly different, with distinctly more bass. 
While adding welcome depth and presence to the music, a more powerful 
bass introduces a perceptual ambig uity to a recording from which other 
characteristic noises, such as the thud of hammers on strings, have been 
rounded off or filtered away. The dual perspective is a characteristic Stock­
hausen ambiguit y. Either the aim of a recording is realistic, assuming a 
cushion of distance between the piano and the listener, making extraneous 
noises inaudible, or it is a study in close-up, in which case the sounds of 
hammers and pedals rising and falling are an essential part of the musical 
fabric. The present compromi se resembles a stage performance taking place 
in front of a supersized tv screen depicting a closeup of the artist's hands. 
Himmels-TOr (Heaven's Door) 
2005: Fourth Hour of KLANG. No. 84 (Stockhausen-Verlag; cd SV-86) 
For a percussionist and a little girl. 
Duration: 28'. 
Heaven's Door is a strangely compelling work expressing the same single­
mindedness associated with Helikopter-Streiehquartet t. A solo percussionist 
pounds in varying patterns on an unyielding door incorporating panels of 
woods of different density sounding different notes, like a giant marimba-
510 CHAPTER THIRTY 
phone. A listener is put in mind of Martin Luther nailing the Ninety-five 
Theses to the door of Wurttember g Church, or Black Rod banging on the 
door of the British House of Commons , demanding entry. The work was 
commission ed by an Italian concert organization, the appropriately named 
Angelica, and premiered by the American Stuart Gerber. It is curiously rich 
in allusion to the United States, from the giant marimbas of Harry Partch 
to the old Bob Dylan song of the same title and its refrain "Knock, knock, 
knocking on heaven's door." Harry Partch is said to have constructed a 
staircase in his home on which the barefoot composer would bound up and 
down on alternate steps, sounding different melodies. The notion of passing 
through a wooden door to paradise is also key to the final artwork by Marcel 
Duchamp, Etant donnes, executed in secret over twenty-one years from 1946 
to 1966. 
The notated score is a work of genial simplicity, always a good sign. The 
musical image of an impenetrable barrier revisits the curtain of string 
players in Trans and, like the earlier work, with the suggestion of a hidden 
world behind the barrier portending unrequit ed anguish, violence , and 
menace. Alternate titles considered for Trans at the time were Jenseits 
"Beyond" and Musik fur den nachsten Toten "Music for those about to die." 
At the end, when the wooden door yields and opens, the percussionist 
enters, followed by a little girl, and is lost to view. (I am reminded here of 
Picasso's 1934 image of the little girl leading the blinded Minotaur by the 
hand, even though the percussionist leads and the little girl follows.) What 
ensues are unseen metal sounds of gongs, crashing cymbals, and the wail of 
a pair of sirens, an unexpected caricatur e of Ionisation as if to suggest that 
Varese's instrumentall y identical sound world stood for chaos and destruc­
tion. That the two worlds are related can be shown by cross-fading the two: 
they blend seamlessl y. But in contrast to the coolly disciplined industrial 
aesthetic of a composer Stockhausen once described as a musical father 
figure, the heaven of Himmels-Tur evokes a burned-out wasteland. 
24 Turin 
2006: No. 84 extra (Stockhausen-Verlag; cd SV-86) 
Electronic music from door and rin tones, and speaker. (German and English versions) 
Duration: 13'. 
"Stockhause n's ring tones," the Turin sounds are a wonderful byproduct of a 
recording session of Himmels-Tur in which the composer processed the door 
sounds to a low frequency, and then added rin sounds, likewise transposed 
to low pitch, to add harmonic structure to the resulting quakelike deton­
ations. It is possible, even likely, that the composer had in mind to create 
new and different sounds to add unexpected depth to the hidden sound 
world behind "the door" for a work unfolding up to that point without any 
amplific ation. In the event, the same process is applied to each of the 
wooden tones of the door, to which bell-like spectra of the rin, Japanese 
bowls, are added to create a scale of monume ntal sounds issued as a stand-
LAST RITES 511 
alone composition, each introduced by the composer with an accompanying 
"noble word" naming a virtue or virtuous quality. 
Readers of a certain age may recall sounds of a similar kind from action 
dramas such as CSI Miami, used as musical punctuation or exclamation 
marks signalin g a break in time, the end of one scene and the beginning of 
another. Added interest for a Stockhausen in the present case is imagining 
such sounds as a possible solution to the problem of concentrating an entire 
composition within the timescale of one second or less. 
Harmonien (Harmonies) 
2006: Fifth Hour of KLANG. No. 85 (Stockhausen-Verlag; cd SV-87) 
For solo bass clarinet (85.1; alternative versions for trumpet 85.2 and flute 85.3). 
Duration: 15-16'. 
"Melody to sound -rhythm to vibration" is the composer 's motto for the fifth 
Hour, a work the composer says was inspired by the bass clarinet artistry of 
Suzanne Stephens rehearsing "Libra" from Sirius. Clarinetists will already 
be familiar with the idea of transitionin g from continuous trill-like passages 
at high speed to rhythmicized melodies at moderate or even slow speed, and 
back again to high-speed trills, techniques as sociated with the artist from 
the era of Harlekin and Kleine Harlekin and the butterfly dance of Amour. 
These earlier works, in common with "Libra" and the entire conception of 
Sirius, derive their energy and interest from imitating the transformations 
available to the composer with the EMS sequencer, a voltage-control device 
allowing a melody loop of limited duration to be compressed in time and 
condensed in range until the melody becomes a blur or a Morse-lik e mono­
tone. Adding interest to the process is that as the timescale is compressed, 
the differences in notated durations within the initial melody reduce 
gradually to unity, in a manner resembling Messiaen's mode of contraction 
of a rhythm by a constant value, rather than in constant proportion. The 
present work, and the set of six trios derived from it, are permutations of a 
series of note sequences oscillating like the same tapeloops, from slow to 
very fast, in isolation and in varying combination, as if by the flick of a 
digital switch. Based on arithmetical modes of durations and numbers of 
notes, the macro melody formations in Harmonien reinforce the allusion to 
Messiaen's personna ges rythmiques and the serialist era of the 1950s, along 
(one would hope) with the spirit of optimism of Spiel, Punkt e 1952, and 
Forme/. 
Since these transformation processes are associated with now obsolete 
tape and analogue synthesizer technolog ies, and before them to the tape 
loop timbres and processes of Kontakte, the title "harmonies" may be the 
composer's way of insisting on the natural harmony of the older analogue 
style of continuous transformation of a waveform, a nostalgia for former 
times and processes lost to music through the replacement of analogue by 
digital synthesizers. 
The melodic material of Harmonien is varied and permutat ed in Hours 
512 CHAPTER THIRTY 
6-11, all trios of various combinat ions, some with ancillary players. 
Schonheit (Beauty) 
2006: Sixth Hour of KLANG. No. 86 (Stockhausen-Verlag; cd SV-87) 
For bass clarinet, flute, and trumpet. 
Duration: 30'. 
The title "beauty" is assigned to Stockhausen's char acteristic trio of bass 
clarinet, flute, and trumpet, timbres representing the cardinal wave forms. 
Having dedicated Harmonien to Suzanne Stephens on bass clarinet, Stock­
hausen arranged alternate versions of the same solo work for trumpet and 
flute, and all three are presented on the same cd. A reader is struck at the 
textural similarity of writing with the solo writing of Boulez, starting with 
the solo flute part for the 1973 version of ... Explosante-fixe ... and revived 
with interest in the French composer's analogous run of late works for solo 
flute, clarinet, and electron ics. Both composers adopt a stream of conscious­
ness aesthetic leading to protracted cadenza-like monologues in which the 
role of electronic or ensemble accompaniments is portrayed as enhanced 
resonance. 
Boulez is linked to these latest trios by association with Le marteau 
sans maitre, a work conceived instrumentally as a deconstruction of a lead­
ing timbre, the alto voice, into component characters represented by a range 
of alternate tone-colors and speech elements circulating seemingly indepen­
dently and allowed to combine and recombine. 
For a Boulez as for Debussy, timing is flexible, expressed in terms of 
emotional nuance: nerueux, souple, obstine-while guided by metronome 
indications . Boulez can do this because he is French, and also because he 
has the means of effecting liaisons between the impulsive soloist and the 
attendant ensemble or computer, both of which are primed to adjust their 
entries to the cue of the lead voice. Stockhausen however is dedicated in 
principle to the idea of a tempo scale organized metronomically from MM 60 
to MM 120, an octave higher. At times in the past, from the premiere of 
Kontra-Punkte under Hans Rosbaud to recordings of Punkte 1952-62 under 
Boulez, he has allowed the tempo scale to be shifted by degrees up or down, 
for acoustical or other reasons. While Boulez consistently objected to having 
to adjust a live performance to the preset timing of a tape recording (as in 
Kontakte or Third Region of Hymnen with Orchestra ), Stockhausen saw 
merit in compressing the natural instincts of a player into the strict time­
scale of a supeI'personal intelligence. An exception to the rule, volunteered 
by the composer in conversation at the time of Stockhausen on Music, arose 
while working on the final section of Kontakte: "we had to do it all over 
again, because the general speed was too fast."5 
Traditionally the tempo of a musical performance is a compromise 
arrived at by a combination of natural agility, emotional function (to stim­
ulate a response from an audience), and practical function (expressing a 
text, or following the steps of a dance form). Since instruments differ in tone 
LAST RITES 513 
color and "weight, " they also have different tempo centers, or natural tim­
ings. It follows that assigning the same actions and unyielding metronomic 
timings to a range of solo players is a way of finding out which instruments 
are naturally faster, equal, or slower to adjust. On the cd, flute and trumpet 
versions of Harmonien appear more at ease than the bass clarinet, in this 
case an instrument of distinctly greater range and a version of the score 
demanding perhaps the greatest agility. If this is a competit ion, judging by 
the cd the flute is allowed greatest flexibilit y and almost a minute of extra 
time to complete the course. 
When all three come together, of course, all conform to the same time­
structure , which then becomes a means of establishing a hierarchy among 
the players. Establis hing a hierarchy is a major motivator for the composer, 
so the goal of achieving harmony is inherently defined as a power struggle 
or contest for leadership. 
Balance (Balance) 
2006-7: Seventh Hour of KLANG. No. 87 (Stockhausen-Verlag; cd SV-88) 
For bass clarinet, English hom, and flute. 
Duration: 30'. 
In "Balance," titled unusually in English, the bright-voiced trumpet assoc­
iated with heroism and motivation in the character of Michael in LICHT is 
replaced by the rounder, more concentrated tone of a cor anglais. A situation 
of balance (in German Bilanz, Gleichgewicht, Libra, or Waage) is implicitly 
stable, contented and non hierarchical . The composer's innate mistrust of a 
situation according equal weight to opposing principles or policies underlies 
the actions of Mittwoch aus LICHT, in particular, themes of compromise 
and absence of leadership in the actions of "Welt-Parlament" and "Mich­
aelion." Such thoughts are far from evident in this performance by a trio of 
fellow musicians of considerable fluidity and warmth of interaction who 
bring a delightful, at times bubbling enthusiasm to a work of outwardly 
strenuous formulae. This is an immersive music of well-mat ched timbres, 
including a more open-toned and solistic bass clarinet. One is reminded at 
times of Zeitmasse's sense of humor; trills and runs are beautifully matched 
and executed. From the booklet illustration it appears that the three 
microphones are elevated about 12 feet above the platform, apparently in a 
straight line, classical fashion, perhaps in a triangle formation. 
"Balance" in English has an additional layer of meaning, related to the 
task of a balance engineer in a recording studio. In the absence of specific 
technical data one has to rely on external indications, in the present case a 
fixed instruction that all trios in the present series adopt a triangle form­
ation onstage. It may well be assumed that the triangle is simply decorative, 
but in recording terms such a formation has specific implicat ions. Stock­
hausen will have encountered, at the Club d'Essai in Paris during his 1952 
sojourn, and in widely available technical literatur e of the period, a system 
devised by engineer Jacques Poullin for recording sounds in 3D and moving 
514 CHAPTER THIRTY 
them about in an early form of surround-sound. In an article reprinted by 
Werner Meyer-Eppler in a special edition of Gravesano Review, Poullin 
describes a four-channel system in tetrahedral array consisting of an equi­
lateral triangle of three inward-facing microphones , and one suspended 
above at the center, and a corresponding speaker formation for playback 
purposes . "With four playback channels," Poullin writes, "one can define an 
acoustic space within which it is theoretically possible to create as many 
virtual sound sources as may be desired, by combining the various inten­
sities in appropriate weights from each of the four channels. With a suitable 
arrangement of four speakers a listener facing in any direction has the 
impression of being inside an acoustic environment, unlike a normal concert 
situation where the audience is on one side facing the musicians on the 
platform."6 
The idea of experiencing a composition from both sides of the screen, as 
it were, is already presented in "Hoch-Ze iten" from Sonntag aus LICHT, so 
the composer is admittedly toying with the idea of reinventing the perfor­
mance space. That he is aware of the technical implications we already 
know from Mikrophonie I, which plays with the pseudostereo conseque nces 
of combining sound images from both faces of a giant tam-tam treated in the 
manner of a ribbon microphone , and in 1968 when he mixed down the rear 
channels of Kontakte's electronic music in phase inversion, against the 
advice of DG producers , to preserve the music's original spatiality.7 Hidden 
in the triangular formation of players and microphon es, like a clue to a 
crossword puzzle, is a recording strategy intended to capture a performance 
in 3D like an acoustic hologram. Poullin's setup, of a sophistication hardly 
suitable fo r Schaeffer and the sound materials of musique concrete, included 
a tetrahedral array of matching speakers equipped with curved reflectors 
like bishop's mitres. The challenge of Balance , and by extension for all of the 
trios, is to explore the possibility of uniting three separate instrumen ts into 
a single holophonic entity combining aspects of all three tone colors-a 
harmony of fused identities, not just a harmony of notes.

Hoffnung (Hope) 
2006-7: Ninth Hour of KLANG. No. 89 (Stockhausen-Verlag; cd SV-89) 
For violoncello, viola, and violin. 
Duration: 35'. 
A string trio pursues the unified timbre theme while introducing the gen­
uinely interesting new dimension of instrumental resonance to the theme of 
timescale variation. The violin family differ from the winds in at least two 
important ways: first as sound diffusers, which is their acoustic function in 
an orchestra; second in possessing their own resonance chambers and being 
able to move them about and control the projection and balance of sound to 
a greater extent than winds whose signaling function makes them more 
naturally directional. Strings also have unusual extra resources in tone and 
texture, arising from the fact that they are frictional by nature. A listener 
notices early on that various "colored noises" such as suI ponticello, spiccato, 
and col legno are exploited , but pizzicato is nowhere to be heard. It becomes 
clear that the violinist is using body movement in relation to the micro­
phone as an alternative means of dynamic control. In section III the violin is 
instructed to stand up, raise the violin and repeat the zombie-lik e actions of 
a familiar insert from Trans, and to execute a fade at the end of the trio by 
running off the stage (a comic special effect in honor of Gerard Hoffnung not 
included in the SV recordi ng).

Erwachen (Awakening) 
2006-7: Twelfth Hour of KLANG. No. 92 (Stockhausen-Verlag; cd SV-90) 
For cello, trumpet, and soprano saxophone. 
Duration: 30'. 
An unusual but apt neo-baroque trio combination of three inherently bright 
but contrasting sonorities, expeciall y successf ul because of their complemen­
tary functions: the cello providing warmth, texture, and amb ience, the 
trumpet clarity and multiple muted identities, and the soprano saxophone

and crisp, producing some of the finest staccato chords in the entire series of 
trio combinat ions. At [12] the soprano sax quotes the opening clarinet 
flourish from Integrales by Varese, opening gesture of the handwritten motif 
by the composer dedicated to clarinetist Suzee Stephens and used as cover 
LAST RITES 517 
illustration for the cd. In this recording there appears to be a more relaxed 
attitude to incidental and peripheral noise, especially welcome because such 
natural noises create intimacy while also highlighting difference-a change 
having the effect of redefining the technical goal of "harmony" from the 
elimination of differences to focusing on positive resemblances , by analogy 
with the harmony of vibrating elements of gut, wood, and metal jointly 
contributing to the tone quality of a grand piano. 
To understand what is concealed behind the ritual fa�ade of these late 
trios, it helps to be aware of their relation to similar earlier works. In 
relation to Sonntags Abschied for example, the instrumentation for five 
synthesizers and title "Strahl en" meaning "streams of radiant light," given 
the terminology of the opera series as a whole, evoke expectations of a 
dazzling image of modulated incandesc ent sound streamin g to the ends of 
the universe. Following exchanges of messages via central command bet­
ween widely separated string players in "Helikopter-Streichquartett, n the 
choice of five synthesizers raises the interesting prospect of a network of 
senders and receivers entailing frequency modulation between the players, 
a music of signals transmit ted and received, and also modified before being 
passed on. Similar processes are at work at the climax of Boulez's Repons, 
from the moment when a magic circle of six keyboard soloists initiates an 
exchange of messages with one other and a central computer and receive 
different messages, permutatio ns, by return. What that coup de theatre is 
bound to suggest to a rival of Stockhausen's caliber is the imminent reality 
of a multi voice polyphony in which each player has the ability simply by 
playing to influence the sonic output of others: not just in counterpoint in 
the old sense, but in signals acting as control modulations affecting the 
speech of others. Repons's amiable charade of artificial intelligence in dia­
logue with a forum of well-tempered keyboardists draws profoundly, I have 
no doubt, on the famous example of Joseph Weizenbaum's ELIZA software 
by which an artificial int elligence appears to engage in conversation with a 
medical patient. 
For a Stockhau sen, already experienced with ring modulation, to be 
able to match Boulez's achievement by composing and combining melody 
formations to influence the transmission of other melodies carrying inform­
ation such as Morse code, or corresponding to elements, numbers , or other 
data, represents a natural extension of his formula compositions of the mid-
1970s into multiple new dimensions. He had attempted as much as recently 
as Mittwochs-Abschied, in which the spatialit y of the tape part of Orchester­
Finalisten is effectively turned inside out. 
For the musicologist, extended immersion in Harmonien and each of the 
six trios may appear a daunting assignment, not altogether helped by a 
lingering suspicion that the composer's fixed and ultimate intention is a 
didactic equivalent of Hindemith's Ludus Tonalis, or the 24 preludes and 
fugues of Shostakovich . For individual instrumentalists involved directly in 
only one or two of the set, the more interesting task lies in discovering ways 
of merging sonic identities, in the manner of select mixture stops of an 
invisible organ (or harmonium). To achieve that degree of tonal fusion in a 
518 CHAPTER THIRTY 
trio of unlike instruments , experience of studio recording and mixing down 
will naturally help, since critiquing a recording develops a perception of one­
self simultaneously as executant and also as an ingredient of an ensemble 
totality. Building on that dual perception also implies experience of a range 
of different microphone types. 
Both the Club d'Essai of Paris Radio, under Schaeffer, and the Elec­
tronic Music Studios of Cologne Radio under Herbert Eimert, were installed 
in the radio drama suites of their respective organizations, where there was 
already a longstanding culture of solo and group choreography of voices in 
dynamic relation to fixed microphone configurations. Of particular import­
ance was the ribbon microphone invented in 1931, which has the peculiar 
virtue of being sensitive to sound on either face of the capsule, but 
insensitive at 90 degrees to either side, edge-on to the ribbon. The rapid fall­
off of sensitivity of a figure of eight polar diagram allows the actor to move 
easily "on and off mic" by a turn of the head, a method of volume control by 
the actor without the balance engineer having to change the fader setting. 
During the 1930s, by aligning two such microphones vertically facing left 
and right at 90 degrees, an early form of surround sound was devised, out of 
which the Poullin tetrahedral array was later developed. By placing three 
identical ribbon microphones in line between the three players, all facing 
the center, and positioning an omnidirectional microphone above, at the 
apex of the tetrahedron facing downward, a system is set in place where 
each soloist is directly on-mic to the microphon e opposite, and off-mic to 
those on either side, while the whole sound field is captured and integrated 
by the microphone suspended above. 
In the present set of official recordings, what photographic evidence 
there is suggests that despite being recorded in the same studio under the 
same excellent technician, no attempt has been made to employ a consistent 
microphone setup; instead, the balance engineer has followed best practice 
in selecting and positioning microphones in each case for the instruments in 
question. But if a common purpose is behind the design of these different 
trios, as well as their symmetries and marginal differences, the possibility 
arises of a more deliberately artificial approach to production based on a 
uniform close-mi crophone array with a view to creating hybrid sounds com­
bining characteristics of all three instruments . In Adieu (1966) for example, 
an overall soft dynamic is combined with close microphone recording in 
order to capture and blend the subtle interactions of wind instruments glid­
ing microtonally in and out of tune with one another. A similar process is 
already in play in Stimmung, whose six rather than three voices, arranged 
in a circle facing one another, each holding a personal microphone, are re­
quired to vocalize sounds intended to influence one another. 
CHAPTER THIRTY-ONE 
Cosmic Pulses 
Completed in 2007 with the participation of Kathinka Pasveer and Antonio 
Perez AbelIan, Cosmic Pulses was planned from the outset to resemble the 
roar of a lion, or a rocket liftoff. From the late 1950s of Zyklus, Carre, and 
Kontakte, Stockhausen had been fascinated by the idea of sounds in rotation 
and how to realize them in a technical sense, whether orchestrally in Carre, 
choreogra phically in Zyklus by having the performer rotate on axis, or elec­
tronically rotating sounds on tape by means of an array of loudspeakers . 
The 1984 electronic vortex of Kathinkas Gesang, realized at IRCAM, trans­
lated the concept of being carried aloft in a tornado into the digital domain, 
while rubbing textures smooth and iridescent in stark contrast to the physi­
cality of Kontakte, or magical reality of Luzifers Abschied , where electronics 
are set aside in favor of the sound of massed clogs running at speed around 
the galleries of a church. 
The work can also be described mischievously as "Stockhausen's spin 
cycle": a rotating sound mass of twenty-four independently spinning frequ­
ency layers, effectively an inflected tempered scale, building gradually layer 
by layer to full density, then shedding layer by layer until only the highest 
and most rapid rotations are left, and they too vanish. The structure looks 
back to Formel, the effect however is overwhelming and also exhilarating, a 
bit like being carried aloft by a tornado, falling down a rabbit hole, or being 
pulled into a rotating black hole, to emerge who knows where. Like laun­
dered contents after a spin cycle, the listener emerges from Cosmic Pulses 
feeling refreshed, squeaky clean, even a little damp. 
As is often the case, behind the storybook fa�ade lies a core of engin­
eering science relating to the dynamics of fluid flow, fundamental processes 
underlying speech and wind music producti on. The art of music originated 
from studies of force and resistance in nature leading to the release of ener­
gy in controllable tones. The interest of modeling air or fluid flow wit hin, 
say, a hollow tube like a flute or clarinet, is not only knowledge of value to 
engineers and the medical profession, but raises more general philosophical 
issues concerning the effects of turbulence and transformation of chaotic 
motion, represented by noise, into structured motion represented by tones of 
520 COSMIC PULSES 
constant pitch. The aesthetic attraction of converting raw energy into struc­
tured tone is that the latter, by nature periodic, is easier to hear and more 
efficient and penetrating for communicat ion. A musician earns valuable 
status within the tribe through mastering the art of converting spent 
(exhaled) energy into coherent, controllable energy. 
Cosmic Pulses 
2007: Thirteenth Hour of KLANG. No. 93 (Stockhausen-Verlag; cd SV-91) 
Electronic music. 
Duration: 32'. 
Cosmic Pulses is a study in turbulence to be compared, in that sense, to 
nineteenth-century art depicting storms, raging torrents, or waterfalls. In 
this case, however, we are dealing with a manufactured turbulence closer 
perhaps to a computer model of the atmosphere of Jupiter and dynamics of 
the Great Red Spot, a continental mass of circulatin g gas that somehow 
survives the tidal forces of the planet spinning on its axis. A composition of 
twenty-four layers rotating at different speeds has an obviously speculative 
dimension. A page in James Gleick's Chaos describes the process by which a 
fluid trapped between rotating inner and fixed outer cylinders transforms 
spontaneously into a layered structure, known as a Couette-Taylor flow, the 
stable layers of which are harmonio usly related.l Since Cosmic Pulses is 
layered by design, the point of interest in a musical simulation is to find out 
whether the layers spontaneously integrate into a super-cell of rotational 
energy, reach a condition of stable harmony, or spontaneously self-destruct, 
an uncertainty of outcome making the new work an example of "exploratory 
experime ntation" in the style of Goethe, rather than empirical science in the 
tradition of Newton. The nature of the experiment and off-the-shelf quality 
of the sound materials employed, together indicate a return to the spirit of 
inquiry of Electronic Studies I and II of 1953-54, and reversion to an aes­
thetic of analogue manipulation of sound. 
Cosmic suggests the supernatural, immense rotational motion of the 
Ptolemaic cosmos of ancient times, mirrored in the harmonic series of the 
Pythagorean monochord. It does not refer to the signature melodies or trills 
played by live performers, whose movement is simply descriptive of the 
influence of the unseen cosmic voice disturbing them into motion. Pulses in 
the title denotes a periodically interrupted flow of energy, like a Helmholtz 
siren, which at a certain threshold is audible as a tone of constant pitch. 
Pulsed tone is intermittent, whereas digitally synthesized tone is typically 
continuous. Human speech is the product of a pulse mechanism creating a 
noise in the throat which is modified by the acoustics of the mouth cavity to 
enhance certain partial frequencies and suppress others. Speech in human 
beings is created out of continuously moving soft, malleable tissue, whereas 
birds and insects such as cicadas communicate over proportionally greater 
distances by rapid friction or drummin g actions against an external hard 
material resonator. The interaction of pulsed and continuous waveforms is 
CHAPTER THIRTY-ONE 521 
famously illustrated in Kontakte at Moment X, 17' 0,5" in the score. 
The idea of a composition of layers, each of which pulsates irregularly in 
different patterns, originates with the vocoder introduced to Werner Meyer­
Eppler by inventor Homer Dudley of Bell Labs visiting Bonn in 1948. The 
meeting inspired Meyer-Eppler to press for the setting up of an electronic 
music studio at Cologne Radio. The effect of filtering a speech signal into 
pulsed layers, then recombining them to cause the voice magically to reap­
pear, is demonstrated in two short studies, "Musik und Sprache" and "Zu 
Ehren von Igor Stravinsky," featuring the speaking voice of Herbert Eimert, 
made between 1955 and 1957 and issued by Wergo on vinyl in 1963 as part 
of the compilation "Einfiihrung in die elektronische Musik" (WER 60006). 
In Cosmic Pulses Stockhausen is returning to his roots and attempting 
to emulate a process he had refused to entertain at the time of Gesang der 
Jilnglinge because the vocoder had contributed to the Allied war effort as a 
speech encryption system. His apparent aim is to employ different combina­
tions from an eight-channel speaker system to mimic the internal resonan­
ces of speech on an enormous scale, treating the entire concert hall acoustic 
as a supersized vocal cavity containing localized zones of specific bandwidth 
or formant resonance. Any live music presented within such a system will 
be perceived in tremulously modulated form as the equivalent in scale of 
peripheral noise at the edges of divine speech, like the "tinkling cymbals" of 
Old Testament lore. 
Meyer-Eppler was undoubtedly familiar in 1955 with the RCA Mark I 
Synthesizer newly unveiled in the United States. Designed by Harry Olson 
and Hubert Belar, the RCA desig n adopted by Milton Babbitt at Columbia­
Princeton incorporated a white noise generator and tunable filter bank, sup­
posedly for synthesizing cymbal, triangle, rattle, and drum sounds (which 
are basically different bandwidths of white noise with more or less added 
reverbera tion). In his Die Reihe I paper recommending filtered white noise 
as a simple means of creating a more convincing tremulant effect, Meyer­
Eppler is focusing on white noise in the infrasound range as a source for 
modulating cinema organ tone in the audible range. Its implication for a 
complex speaker setup such as Cosmic Pulses is that infrasound frequencies 
among clusters of speakers will set up organic but unpredictable tremolo 
oscillations capable of modulating live action music on the platform, an 
effect varying from listener to listener depending on the seat location in the 
concert chamber. 
That Stockhau sen commissioned the mixdown of Cosmic Pulses tone 
material into layers from the same team responsible in 1977 for the opening 
and closing rotations of Sirius suggests he imagined the two processes to be 
created in the same way. However in Sirius the dancing standing wave 
effects were externally imposed on the electronic music content by the latter 
being rotated at audible speed around an eight-channel speaker system. 
The 24 layers of Cosmic Pulses rotate in periodicities varying from MM 
1.17 to MM 240, in frequency terms deep in the subaudio range to a high of 
ca. 4 hertz, a threshold at which the body starts to react uncontrol lably. 
This is potentially dangerous territory typically associated with high energy 
522 COSMIC PULSES 
death metal music employing infrasound, a zone with potential for physical 
harm mitigated in the present case by maintaining the various layers in 
constant circulation among a multi-speaker sound system. The "flying sau­
cer" arrivals and departur es of Sirius are very different from Kontakte's four 
channel rotations in 1960, Sirius's denser sounds spontaneously giving rise 
to siren-like interference effects perceived as standing columns of shim­
mering sound, varying in frequency with the slightest head movement of the 
individual listener. There can be little doubt that the increased density and 
complexity of voices in Cosmic Pulses were calculated to build on these "out 
of body" audio eff ects, and perhaps add to them. 
In real life a speeding racecar driving around a circular track is contin­
uously audible from a point in the center, its sound varying in quality and 
loudness with speed, direction, and distance relative to the listener. A sound 
system of fixed speakers, on the other hand, like the pillars of Stonehenge , 
reflects the continuous flow of a passing sound as a stream of pulses, 
opening and closing as the sound passes by, and at extreme speed genera­
ting their own tone, like a siren or electronic impulse generator modulating 
the wave-form of a passing signal. In the small-scale, closed environment of 
a concert hall, interference effects of this kind are compound ed, softened, 
and blurred unpredictably by delayed reflections from side walls and ceiling, 
though in special backdrops such as the fractal surfaces and domed interior 
of a gothic cathedral, interesting acoustical results can be achieved . Without 
trials, a desired result is impossible to guarantee: all a concept work can do 
is advertise the possibilit ies. 
The deliberately limited, even banal, tonal material and absence of fin­
ish of Cosmic Pulses may be defended on grounds of lack of time, but on the 
plus side, an absence of distinguishing aesthetic qualities (all subsumed in 
the pearly iridescence characteristic of manufactured sonorities) obliges an 
interpreter to focus on an underlying structural reality, its nakedness lend­
ing the present work a constructivist aesthetic, an acoustical Tatlin's Tower 
spiraling upward into the unknown. 
To describe the electronic sound materials as banal is simply to say that 
while typical of the synthesizer in question, they bear little relation to the 
serial properties implied by the score plan, attaining neither the tactile 
richness of Kontakte, nor the gritty immediacy of Hymnen or Kurzwellen, 
which freely incorporate the realistic distortions and intermodulations of 
short-wave radio. Produced on a commercial synthesizer with what appear 
to be largely existing presets (from Sonntags-Abschied) transposed in time 
and pitch to a largely theoretical serial prescription, and subsequently 
mixed down in strata of three layers at a time, this churning electronic 
music displays an outwardly elegant consistency of finish but little variety 
to compare with (say) the noisy organ mixtures of Messiaen's visionary "Les 
yeux dans les roues" from the Livre d'Orgue. 
The argument in favor of consistency of timbre across the range is that 
it encourages a good blend of individual voices or layers in any combination , 
but consistency of timbre is not guarant eed simply by scaling the same mat­
erial or patch up and down. Organ pipes forming a scale of different sizes 
CHAPTER THIRTY·ONE 523 
have to be individuall y voiced to sound the same and blend together, and 
consorts of the same family of recorders, shawms , or viols differ markedly in 
proportion and "voicing" as well as actual size for the sake of blending as an 
ensembl e. Relying on simple expansion and compression of token waveforms 
is a false convenience, only reinforcing the artificiality of the genre, perhaps 
inevitably given the trend toward increasingly tame and listless synthesizer 
tonalities since the premiere of Freitag and departure of programmer Simon 
Stockha usen from the family firm. 
Historically the combination of powerful sounds and rotating speakers 
has been associated with public sirens warning of imminent attack, in times 
of war for example an air raid, or natural disaster in peacetime. In 1960, 
rotation emerged afresh as an expressive innovation, in Carre where multi­
voice sound complexes are rotated among four choirs and orchestr as, and 
electronic sound among four speakers in Kontakte. Interest in the mechanics 
of rotary movement had been sparked in part by tremulant mechanisms in 
electric organs of the period, the US Allen company employing dual rotating 
speakers mounted on a vertical turntable within the cabinet, and the Leslie 
company a paddle or rotor blade mounted inside the cabinet in front of a 
single loudspeaker to modulat e the sound. The paddle especially "causes a 
cyclic change in both pitch and volume, according to the well-known Doppler 
effect. The sound therefore rises in pitch as the paddle rotates toward the 
observer, and falls when it moves toward the loudspeaker cone," the writer 
adding "Care should be taken not to apply it to loudspeak ers handling very 
low frequencies."2 
In 1961 Oberlin composer Richard Hoffmann, Jr., a former assistant to 
Arnold Schoenber g, published an Orchestra Piece with Universal Edition, 
Stockhausen's publisher, incorporating a part for rotating speaker. At this 
time the WDR studio also acquired a Rotations Lau tsprecher.3 In due course 
Stockhausen composed Momente 1964 for voices and instrumental ensemble 
including Hammond and Lowrey organs, both of which incorporated Leslie 
tremulants. In 1965 Stockhausen revisited the combination of voices and 
Hammond organ in Mikrophonie II, aiming to submit choir voices to real­
time modulation by an equal-tempered keyboard with added tremulant. The 
invariant regularity of theater organ tremulant mechanisms had originally 
prompted Meyer-Eppler to publish his paper in Die Reihe I, on what many 
readers regarded as a topic of esoteric and marginal interest. As a founder 
and coeditor of Die Reihe, Stockhausen read and approved the article for 
publicat ion. The article ends by referring briefly and obliquely to the effects 
of infra sound modulati on.4 
Such an intention of employing one instrument to influence the acoustic 
behavior of voices or other instruments provides a credible basis for the trios 
of the KLANG cycle and their outwardly obsessive back and forth oscill­
ations between single tones and chords, slow counterpoints in the style of 
Messiaen, and high-speed tape loop-style tremolos, contrasting times cales in 
natural interference, and frequency modulation of reverberating tones over 
a scale of frequencies extending from the infrasound up to and beyond the 
upper limit of human hearing. 
524 COSMIC PULSES 
In the past, the rapid passage of sound rotating from speaker to speaker 
in a four-or even eight-speaker configuration was apt to impose a siren-lik e 
combination frequency and amplitude modulation to the signal, typically 
perceived as "flap." Meyer-Eppler's article in Die Reihe proposed to substi­
tute a subaudio "aleatoric" oscillation derived from filtered white noise, to 
both soften the damage and humanize the effect by introducing a subtle 
irregula rity to the amplitude modulation, in keeping with natural speech 
and song pro cesses. After Kontakte and Sirius, and mixed reviews of the 
electronic vortex of "Kathinkas Gesang" in 1983, there are grounds for inter­
preting Cosmic Pulses as a definitive attempt by the composer to implement 
a multi-layered tremulant effect on a massive scale. Typically, Stockhausen 
ensures against failure by overkill, sheer force of numbers overwhelming 
the listener in a final bid to bring the lion's roar to potentially devastating 
life. Like Studie II, the sound complexes of which are unified by natural 
reverberat ion in a studio echo-chamber, Cosmic Pulses ultimately relies on 
the natural ambience of a concert hall to soften and blend the combined 
voices and solo players. 
The essence of Meyer-Eppler's thesis is that in a multi-speaker setup 
both the sound to be modulat ed and the modulating signal should be contin­
uously present in order for the sound to appear realistically to be moving in 
space within an auditorium. There should be no flap effect to interfere with 
the frequency modulation of tone on tone. By varying amplitude levels while 
maintaining a continuous presence of source tones within each cluster of 
speakers (on the principle of a lighthouse maintainin g a steady beam of 
light even while rotating through 360 degrees), the operative signal is no 
longer trapped within the system but ideally continues to oscillate in a 
natural way at all times and amplitudes. This is the critical issue under­
lying the mixdown of layers among selected groups of speakers undertaken 
on the composer 's behalf by Joachim Haas and Grigorio Karman.s 
Stockhausen has compounded problems for himself by employing an 
eight-channel system in variously smaller combinations of oscillating groups 
of 2, 3, 4, and 5 speakers, and insisting on irreg ular trajectories among 
higher numbers of speakers (ironically the effect Meyer-Eppler's aleatoric 
modulation was designed to address automaticall y). For such a system to 
emulate turbulence in nature, the whorls and eddies of a raging torrent, the 
"flap" effect has to be eliminated, because turbulence in a fluid is an effect of 
friction in a continuous medium such as water or air, and the conventional 
approach in Kontakte or Sirius had chosen to interrupt the flow of sound by 
directing it to individual speakers in programmed succession. The successful 
implementation of Stockhausen's plan of constructive interference implies 
the formation of small and large vortices in an overall turbulence, repre­
sented by moveme nts between different speaker collections. To make a 
musical analogy, the twenty-four tone layers of Cosmic Pulses amount in 
effect to partial vibrations of a virtual bell oscillating at different speeds and 
discharging their energies within the resonant structur e represented by the 
speaker system. 
Such interference effects assume what the various gyres and eddies are 
CHAPTER THIRT Y-ONE 525 
programmed to resemble, in other words, the spontaneous disturbance of 
airflow over a wing or streamlined shape placed in a wind tunnel and sub­
jected to wind currents at varying speeds, some of which flow smoothly , 
others forming zones of turbulence. In this case, Stockhausen has taken the 
layers of laminar flow and inserted his own notional turbulence to each in 
the form of inflections of notated melodies. Surprisingly, these are modeled 
on the natural unpredictabilities of speech previously notated in the choir 
parts for Hoch-Zeiten. Whether it is entirely consistent to create an acoustic 
structure for the purpose of generating turbulence, only to manufacture the 
turbulen ce by hand, is the obvious question. The composer's habit of micro­
management of sound is not a bad idea in principle, but in this case the 
effect of manually disturbing the flow of air as it were in advance is to 
suggest that the composer knew on hearing the initial playback of materials 
that his original goal of generating spontaneous aleatoric modulation was 
unlikely to perform as expected. 
Havona 
2007: Fourteenth Hour of KLANG. No. 94 (Stockhausen-Verlag; cd SV-92) 
For bass and electronic music. 
Duration: 24' 10. 
Orvonton 
2007: Fifteenth Hour of KLANG. No. 95 (Stockhausen-Verlag; cd SV-93) 
For baritone and electronic music. 
Duration: 24'. 
Uversa 
2007: Sixteenth Hour of KLANG. No. 96 (Stockhausen-Verlag; cd SV-94) 
For basset-horn and electronic music. 
Duration: 22' 40. 
The Urantia Hours employ a selection of solo instrume nts and voices as live 
offsets to successiv e triple layers of the Cosmic Pulses electronics . The entire 
set follows a logical, albeit mechanical formula assigning voices or instru­
ments to synthesized sounds in an equivalent pitch range from low to high 
in pitch, starting with the bass voice matched to the lowest three electronic 
layers. As the series progresses from low to high pitch levels, the associated 
tempi speed up, as if to suggest an image of heaven as a chirping Messiaen 
aviary surrounded by cicadas by day and kept awake by the squeak of bats 
at night. 
The volume and complexity even of isolated triple layers of electronic 
sound in vigorous counterpoin t is such that the solo player is obliged most of 
the time to do battle, or, like the boy on the burning deck, strive to maintain 
composure in the midst of the surrounding conflagration. While there is 
obvious potential for mutual interference between solo and electronic voices, 
little genuine dialogue appears between them, despite their nominal equiva­
lence of pitch range. At times, the sounds of Havana suggest Boulez's steel 
526 COSMIC PULSES 
pans from Sur Incises; elsewhere however the consistently glassy quality of 
synthesized material adds to the impression of a turbulence contained and 
somehow remote from the reality of actual performance. Perhaps ironically 
for the present case, despite the impression of singing or playing bravely in 
the midst of the maelstrom, in practice to preserve quality a soloist would 
more likely be recorded in isolation from the electronic music, coordinating 
either by listening through headphones (in this case unlikely given the 
intensity and complexity of sound), or on cue from the control room. Just 
how even the bravest soloist can expect to interact meaningfully with the 
music's tongues of fire, and emerge with hair and eyebrows unsinged, 
remains an open question. 
Oruonton for baritone voice is offset by characteristic layers of electronic 
sound in parallel fifths and fourths, in mixtures resembling the timbres of 
Javanese bell plates, tuned bronze flat shapes of distinct pitch. The speed of 
change---<>r rather, degree of turbulence-is noticeably quicker, and the tone 
quality higher and clearer. The baritone voice is nicely matched , a confident 
voiceover singing at a tempo so slow it seems not to matter that the actual 
text material, a resume of reminders and captions , is little more than an 
excuse to have something to say. Words are required in this situation for 
just two reasons: one, to indicate the presence of a human being, and two, to 
provide a human scale against which to gauge the electronic music in the 
background, even when the latter sounds about as threatening as a bundle 
of plastic cutlery rattling in a glass tumbler. There are moments in Orvon­
ton when a listener feel as if trapped on the other side of Heaven's Door, 
aware of urgent pounding on the other side. 
Nebadon 
2007: Seventeenth Hour of KLANG. No. 97 (Stockhausen-Verlag; cd SV-95) 
For horn and electronic music. 
Duration: 21' 42. 
Jerusem 
2007: Eighteenth Hour of KLANG. No. 98 (Stockhausen-Verlag; cd SV-96) 
For tenor and electronic music. 
Duration: 20' 40. 
Nebadon for french horn and electronic music is the first solo in ascending 
sequence to present the solo presence on an equal footing with the synth­
esized background. The reason is straightforward: the horn, eight feet in 
coiled length, is designed to emit a powerful signal over a considerable dis­
tance, so for the first time an instrument is able to challenge the electronic 
sound, added to which the recording in this case is balanced in such a way 
as to match the horn in scale with its sound backdrop. There is a welcome 
assertiveness here, even at the end a sense of genuine triumph, with whoop­
ing high notes. At times the unfazed soloist alternates open and stopped 
sounds, adding to the impression of uninterrupted space. 
In this recording it emerges that the spoken words inserted into the 
CHAPTER THIRTY·ONE 527 
electronic music as performer cues, may also be intended to inject moments 
of connection between performances relayed simultaneously from different 
locations, at a day-long festival, or recorded perhaps for a news documen­
tary report or broadcas t. A technical reason for the improved balance of solo 
horn and electronic sound may be found in the cd booklet photograph of the 
soloist in the studio surrounded (here for the first time) by three ribbon 
microphones in horizontal equilateral triangle formation, as prescribed by 
Poullin, the front microphone just a little elevated. 
Jerusem for tenor and electronics, the latter tuned in parallel minor 
sevenths, pursues the principle of matching the tessitura of the solo voice or 
instrument to the frequency range of the accompanying layers. Such a policy 
would seem to entail emphasizing difference, in preference to blending in, 
previously assumed to be the composer's original goal. That being the case, 
the entire sequence of Urantia hours reflects a fractal concept of acoustics in 
which the same relational formula continues to apply at every scale of 
magnification without end, a fiction calling to mind famously disturbing 
computer-gener ated animations from the 1980s offalling for eternity toward 
a surface in permanent expansion revealing an infinity of identical detail. In 
reality of course we know that there are limits to any scale expansion, from 
the speed of sound and density of air, via the relative flexibility of materials 
subject to vibration at increasing frequency, to the point where substance 
dissolves into molecular configurat ions, and molecules to electric charges of 
variable polarity. 
The tenor voice in the official recording is capable and eloquent, but the 
demanding solo part has been equalized to a point where it has acquired a 
persistent high frequency peak. The distortion is of a kind that could not be 
attributed to a singer subject to freedom of movement in front of a micro­
phone, so must have occurred at the mixing desk. What it suggests is that 
periods of continuous exposure to the electronic music within the narrow 
confines of a mixing suite may have created a ringing in the ears leading to 
overcompensation of the voice signal. (The ringing effect from close listening 
to Cosmic Pulses can persist for a day or more.) One assumes an intention to 
blend the live voice with the prerecorded sonorities in order to convey an 
impression of "an angel singing within the fiery furnace," the boy treble in 
Gesang der Junglinge , or the choir of the Ascension scene in Donnerstag aus 
LICHT, angels "perpetually in transit" (auch Engel sind immer unterwegs). 
Or in spirit, the Indianerlieder duos collectively titled "Am Himmel wandre 
Ich" (In the sky I am walking). In all three cases the point, it appears , is to 
distinguish the singer from the surrounding turbulence, not allow the voice 
to be submerged or consumed .

For soprano saxophone and electronic music.

Paradies (Paradise) 
2007: Twenty-first Hour of KLANG. No. 101 (Stockhausen-Verlag; cd SV-99) 
For flute and electronic music. 
Duration: 18' 02. 
Urantia, for soprano voice, is offset by electronic layers in parallel fourths. 
In the cd recording bass frequencies are noticeably lifted, the voice singing 
against the flow in slow-motion chant. This female voice and music compare 
directly with the boy soprano in Gesang der Jiinglinge . The soprano voice in 
this recording is Kathinka Pasveer, a spirit likewise undisturbed by the 
turbulence carrying on around her and self-evidently the sort of voice one 
would want to hear on the line in the event of a major crisis. The point is not 
entirely frivolous, given Pasveer's crucial role in Stockhausen's later life and 
the vivid symbolism of this particular composition as a representation of the 
passage of the soul toward the bright light at the end of the tunnel depicted 
by Hieronymus Bosch in Paradise: Ascent of the Blessed (1504). 
Edentia for soprano saxophone and electronics features high, crystalline 
timbres against the naturally shrill quality of the saxophone . Despite an 
abundance of high frequencies , the solo instrument is recorded with a 
spaciousness for the first time clearly attributable, judging by the cd booklet 
photograph, to a spaced tetrahedral array: two microphones vertically at 90 
degrees in front of the soloist, and two more horizontally at ca. 10 feet high 
behind him. 
Paradies, its electronic layers alternating between major ninth and 
tenth, is the fastest circulating patterns of the series, its twinkling two-and 
three-speaker oscillations flickering like the wheels of a pocket watch. This 
paradise is a busy environment in which the solo flute effortlessly loops and 
flutters, but has little leisure to soar or glide. 
Here the work ends. No notes are preserved relating to any planned Hours 
22, 23, or 24, and it is not easy to conceive of stages ascending higher than 
Paradise, though a few hardbitten bloggers continue to speculate on possible 
hidden reasons (given that ascending to heaven is not "a cycle" in any sense 
of the term) for announcing a suite of twenty-f our works and delivering only 
twenty-one. 
A reader has a number of options. First and most obvious, the composer 
did not have time: he died bef ore the final three works could be composed. 
The objection to that straightforward explanation is that there is no evid­
ence that he was preparing to compose the missing works. Second, that the 
missing works, representing higher states of being, "exist" invisibly and in­
audibly in a neverending state, a thought ingeniously invoking Hindemit h's 
Das Unaufhorliche as capstone to Schoenberg's Die Jakobsleiter. That does 
CHAPTER THIRTY-ONE 529 
no harm and is a neat thought acknowledging the roles of the two composer s 
in Stockhausen's early musical upbringing. 
Third, the number 21 has meaning for the composer. It is the sum of the 
arithmetical series 1 + 2 + 3 + 4 + 5 + 6 = 21, the numerical basis of the 
hexachord , and is also the sixth term in the Fibonacci series 1,2,3,5,8, 13, 
21, the basis of structural proportion in Bart6k and Le Corbusier. Twenty­
one is 7 x 3, the symbolism of seven days and three characters in LICHT 
requirin g no explanat ion. In music, Schoenberg's Pierrot Lunaire , a cycle of 
3 x 7 poems, and Stockhausen's Momente, a decision tree or mobile of 3 x 7 
branches grouped around three musical attributes also alluding to dimen­
sions of time: timbre, melody, and duration . The number 21 for all these 
reasons is already complete : by extension, the remaining three hours imply 
a false conclusion, or the tristropha, the fifties convention, now dated, of 
indicating incomplet ion, as in the titles" ... explosante-fixe ... " by Boulez, 
or" ... wie die Zeit vergeht ... " by Stockhausen. 
Looking back, the trios and Urantia solos of KLANG are clearly two 
different species. What they share in common is a concern to address the 
challenge of modulating sound with sound either by live acoustical inter­
action, or electroacoustically. The electronic keyboards Stockhausen refused 
to use on his arrival at Cologne Radio in 1952-the Bode melochor d and 
Trautwein monochord , purchased at great expense, as well as wishing to 
have nothing to do with the vocoder-obliged the young composer to create 
new timbres from scratch rather than make use of someone else's patches.6 
He was all the same influenced by makers such as Trautwein who offered a 
range of tone qualities based on weighted combinations of fundamental 
waveforms produced by simple electrical circuits. These fundamental sine, 
square, sawtooth, and ramp waveforms are represented in LICHT by the 
familiar instrumental characters of flute, clarinetlbasset-horn, trumpet, and 
trombone, to which the violin family are finally admitted as alternative 
ramp waveforms in the KLANG cycle. 
The logic of defining a vocabular y of basic waveforms in live instrumen­
tal terms is driven by the idea of composing and manipulating tone mix­
tures through a method of polyphonic switching in which the performers are 
free to assume control and capable of achieving a degree of subtlety impos­
sible by means of an electronic keyboard. A precedent for such a live syn­
thesis procedure already existed in embryo in the attenuated klangfarben­
melodie of Webern. In a vast portfolio of works produced over fifty years, 
Stockhausen developed and refined a range of techniques necessary for live 
intermodulation. They included microphone and filtering techniques and 
notations (Mikrophonie I), ring modulation (Mixtur), frequency modulation 
(Telemusik), microtonal notations for wind instruments (Xi, Susani), inflec­
tional notations for voice (Hoch·Zeiten), mutes and glissandi for trumpet 
(Michaels Reise), changing the acoustic layout of the orchestra (lnori), rota­
tion of the performer at varying sp eed (Harlekin), choreography of mutually 
orbiting players (Bassetsu Trio), mutual interference of amplified voices in 
virtual space (Stimmung), and mutual interference of opposed voices in real 
space (lndianerlied er). Given that history, it is not only logical to interpret 
530 COSMIC PULSES 
the trios and solos of KLANG as essays in live timbre synthesis, it is 
inevitable that they should be interpreted jointly by players, producers, and 
balance engineers from such a perspective in years to come. 
Purely from a sound design perspective, the KLANG trios make the con­
sistent point that, under the special conditions represented by the triangu­
lar formations, it should be possible for each threesome of players to create 
compatible (i.e., harmonious) hybrid acoustic holograms reproducible in a 
3D speaker array. In real terms, the triangle pattern acknowledges that the 
pattern of sound radiated around an instrument varies according to mater­
ial, shape, and intensity by frequency: in a violin, from front and back, sides, 
and f-holes; in a bass clarinet, from the mouth area, open finger holes, and 
upturned bell , and so on. Because the lobes or patterns of energy radiation 
are specific and complicated, the range of frequencies where positive inter­
ference is most likely to occur covers wavelengths corresponding to the 
dimensions of a person, a region from around 5 feet 6 inches (corresponding 
to C an octave below middle C) to about 4 inches (the note A at the top of the 
piano keyboard). When players are choreographed in solo, duos, trios, or 
quartets, the speed and quality of movements invariably have spatial and 
dynamic consequences to be considered both from a technical perspective in 
front of a microphone, and also from an interactive perspective within a 
reproduced sound field that may include other players. When Stockhausen 
instructs the first violin in Hoffnung to stand up, raise his violin, and "exit 
the stage running" it is not just for fun (a play on the name of Gerard 
Hoffnung, founder of the Hoffnung Festivals in Britain in the late 1950s), 
but setting a specific task for the studio production team to reproduce the 
movement of the sound in acoustic space in three dimensions . There may 
yet be ways of achieving the desired refinement of interaction and overcome 
the hurdle of sound being normally invisible, rendering the present choreo­
graphed formations as largely symbolic. One might start by attaching 
lightweight laser pointers or miniature LEDs to instruments indicating the 
locations and directions of sound radiation, in the hope of bringing greater 
precision to pair interactions and incidentally introducin g a space-age dim­
ension of pairs of musicians dueling with light sabers. 
In 2004 Stockhausen took time out to orchestrate five of the Zodiac 
melodies for small orchestra, with the title Funf Sternzeich en. Then in 2007 
he orchestrated five more, titling them Funf weitere Sternzeichen (Five more 
star signs), finishing the second set of five on the evening of December 4, 
succumbing to heart failure the following morning, December 5, 2007. The 
two collections are issued on cd SV-100. Both are completely charming. For 
some inscrutable reason I am reminded of the Stravinsky orchestrations of 
Eight Instrumental Miniatures of 1962, which like Stockhausen revisit 
images of childhood, reinventing their plain melodies in luminous mixtures 
of instrumental color. Of the two sets, the 2004 collection remains true to 
the aphoristic nature of the original melodies and is effortlessly enchanting 
on the ear. The final set, following a period of unremitting intense work, are 
sharp, vital, funny, and impatient as ever.

Born in New Zealand , Robin Maconie studied piano with Christina Geel and 
read English literature and music at Victoria University of Wellington 
under Frederick Page and Roger Savage. A government bursary enabled 
him to study under Olivier Messiaen at the Paris Conservatoire 1963-1964, 
after which a grant from the Deutscher Akademischer Austauschdienst took 
him to Cologne to take part in courses in composition, electronic music, and 
interpretation under Karlheinz Stockha usen, Herbert Eimert, Bernd-Alois 
Zimmermann, Henri Pousseur, Georg Heike, Aloys Kontarsky, and others. 
He has held teachin g appointments at the universities of Auckland, Sussex, 
Surrey , the City Universit y in London, and Savannah College of Art and 
Design . As occasional music correspondent for the Daily Telegraph and 
Times Educational Supplem ent, with the composer 's encourag ement he 
embarked on The Works of Karlheinz Stockhausen (1976), the first critical 
overview in English of a living composer, also one of the most difficult and 
controvers ial composer s ever to have lived. A second edition (1990) was 
followed in 2005 by the first edition of Other Planets, published by Scare­
crow Press, a project brought to completion by the present volume following 
the composer's death in 2007. Previously in 1978 Robin Maconie devised 
and coauthor ed Tuning In, a radical television documentar y on the 
composer produced by Barrie Gavin for the BBC and released in 1980, since 
made available on YouT ube. In 1989 he published Stockhausen on Music, a 
collection of lectures and interviews with the composer that remains a 
popular reference. 
Robin Maconie retired to New Zealand in 2002 and lives in Dannevirke 
in the North Island, where he continues investigations into the history of 
the 20th-century avant-garde and electronic media.
